utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, good morning, Mr. Robinson. I was told that you have something to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Good morning, Mr. President. I'm asking for some assistance from the Trial Chamber, sorry to bother you with this. Last night when we went to the Detention Unit, myself and General Radinovic, in order to prepare for the testimony of -- the cross-examination of Dr. Butler, Dr. Karadzic wasn't allowed to meet us in the privileged room where we have privileged visits. We went ahead and had the visit anyway although we're concerned whether or not any confidentiality was breached, but we went ahead and had the meeting so as not to delay the cross-examination or seek to delay the cross-examination. But Dr. Karadzic would like the Chamber to inquire or use its good offices to inquire with the UNDF as to why he was unable to have a privileged meeting with myself and his expert, and also part of that is there's a room set aside for privileged meetings which has a telephone in which Dr. Karadzic was hoping to contact our investigator during the course of that meeting and get some information and was unable to do that. So we would appreciate it if the Trial Chamber could inquire with the UNDF -- UNDU to determine why we were unable to have a confidential meeting and also to see that that doesn't occur in the future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you were not told about any reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. The personnel that were on duty last night told us that they didn't have any discretion or information as to the reason and they were unable to assist us any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can I just inquire, Mr. Robinson, why did you think that confidentiality might have been breached? Because of the presence of a third party?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, because we were placed in a room that is monitored or can be monitored. Normally we meet in the special room where it is not monitored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson, the Chamber will take a look into the matter. Shall we bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you. Could I have 23703, please. That's a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, that's not in your binders. I'm going back now to a question from His Honour Judge Kwon at 27485 yesterday about the meaning of the name Barijera, which appeared in the conversation between Mr. Karadzic and General Zivanovic which we saw, which for the record is P04484. First let me ask you, did code-names change during the war, for example, names like Badem, Palma, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They should have. What normally happens is that for a particular operation, each relevant headquarters is assigned a new code-name, and many documents that you will see, particularly when you're talking about tactical communications, will show that. Having said that, while that is the proper way in a communications security sense it should have been done, in many cases individuals reverted back to code-names that they had used before previously, so they did not exercise good communications security. So while the correct answer is yes, they should have changed every operation, in reality they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This document is undated and, Your Honours, I did provide it to my colleagues beforehand. It wasn't on the list but it came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We see on the top: National defence state secret, Drina. If you could look at number 3 it states: Main Staff of the RS, command post Barijera; number 4, Main Staff of the RS army rear command post Barijera-1; and number 5, Main Staff of RS army or forward command post Barijera-2. Could you just -- it's pretty self-evident, but on this document does it appear that Barijera is a code-name for the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, on this document it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4938, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Back to where we were, Mr. Butler, on 12 July. If I could have 65 ter number 01945. That's in tab 60 of the first binder, Mr. Butler. I'll tell you that just simply due to time constraints I'm -- you please continue to give full, complete answers, but I'm going to try to make mine shorter and move a little quicker. So here we have another MUP report to Tomo Kovac and the head of public security, again from Dragan Kijac, and it refers to various topics, the liberation of rest of Srebrenica. At the bottom, agreement to evacuate civilians from Potocari. And on page 2, at the top of the English: "It should be noted that among the people staying in Potocari there were hardly any men fit for fighting." So again if you could just give us your view of the significance, if any, of this report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Well, first of all, it reflects that the military and the state security organs are continuing to talk with each other. You can tell in particularly the second paragraph they are repeating information which we know the military security sources have been talking about as well. It reflects -- and again not only the military security, Mr. Vasic is talked about. The same situation with respect to the situation in Potocari. They're continuing to collect against the various NGOs with respect to other issues. So it does represent a continuum of reporting on the pertinent situation that is occurring at that time that is being sent from those individuals on the ground to the senior leadership of both the army and the political organs of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I tender that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4939, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 2016, please. That's the next document in your binder, Mr. Butler. This is sent from the Drina Corps intelligence department on 12th [Realtime transcript read in error "4th"] of July. It's from General Tolimir, chief of security and intelligence on the Main Staff, and I'm interested in the distribution list of who it's going to which includes the same theme we're on, RDB state security and the Ministry of the Interior of the RS and MUP RS. So could you please just comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. Which tab is it again, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, 61.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular document, while it originates from the command of the Drina Corps, you note on the second page it's signed in the name of General Tolimir. At this point this time, on the 12th of July, I believe, General Tolimir is actually at the Drina Corps headquarters in Vlasenica. It reflects his awareness of the situation that is occurring on the road on 12 July 1995. It reflects the fact that they are gaining information from radio intercepts of what they believe the situation is with the column and the objectives of the column. It talks about some other issues related to, you know, their understanding of what they believe the Muslim wishes to portray Srebrenica as. And then finally looking at the distribution list, it reflects the fact that not only is General Tolimir ensuring that key individuals such as General Krstic and Colonel Popovic who are at other locations at this time receive this message, the military and state security organs and the MUP are also addressees on this message. So again reflecting that continued effort between both the army, the MUP, and state security to ensure that each has the most accurate picture of what is going on in the battle-field area. It's an excellent example of how -- how all three parties are working hard to ensure that all of the key decision-makers have the appropriate situational awareness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a follow-up question. Not necessarily speaking just of this document but the ones we've looked at and all the various reports you've reviewed in your work, the VRS, MUP, state security. How quickly, how close to real time is this information being shared between the various organs you've just described?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As quickly as possible. Now, obviously there are going to be delays in passing the information as there is a required processing time with respect to physically writing a report or physically transmitting that report over the existing communications networks and dealing with whatever slight malfunctions or retransmissions have to occur as part of that chain, but when you dovetail this against the intercepted telephonic communications, you see that in many cases even though they are writing these reports, either before the report or as the report is being done, they're also telephonically notifying many of these same correspondents of the same information. So they're not strictly relying on written reports in order to give everyone the appropriate situational awareness. These individuals realise that this information is potentially time sensitive and are making additional efforts to reach out via the telephonic network to call and ensure that they have this information or at least as much of the information as they can pass over the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you can scroll back the transcript. Page 5, line 10. It is recorded that you stated that this was sent from Drina Corps intelligence department on the 4th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I hope I said 12th of July, but it should be 12 July. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in your opinion, this is sent by General Tolimir from Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe at this time General Tolimir is at the Drina Corps when he sends this, and this is why even though it is from General Tolimir, it is sent using a Drina Corps message address header. And in fact, it uses the number strictly confidential 17/897, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we see that second page, page 2. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which corresponds to other reports coming out of the Drina Corps command intelligence department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And this second page is consistent with your observation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This will be admitted as Exhibit P4940.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I now have 65 ter number 23519. That's the map book. I'd like to look at map E27, which is at e-court page 34 it should be with the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'll tell you while that's coming up, Mr. Butler, this is the map you've seen before, a portion of it, which has notations on it written by General Krstic. You see the top one is for 12 July. "Srebrenica has been Serbian and remains Serbian, 12 July 1995, Major-General Rad Krstic," and below, similar notation for 27 July 1995. Can you just tell us the significance of the dates of these two entries made by General Krstic in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12 July 1995 entry was made at -- in a -- in a similar manner I've testified in another case of a map with General Mladic at this 12 July 1995 planning meeting that occurred at the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade where the VRS began planning to undertake the next set of military operations which were designed against Zepa. It was the Stupcana 95 plan. My understanding of the signature on 27 July 1995 is that on that particular date, that is when the VRS in their mind designated the completion and the capture of the -- of the Zepa safe area. So again, both of those things by General Krstic to note those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. At this time, Your Honours, I would tender the map book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Can I hear from you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't have any objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In its entirety, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4941, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Butler, that was the last document I was going to show for the events of 12 July. Now I'm moving on to a chapter of the 13th of July, events of that day and related documents. So the first one I'd like to show you is 65 ter 1931. That's at your tab 66, Mr. Butler. And it's the report by General Vasic -- sorry, Chief Vasic referring to a meeting with General Mladic in which Chief Vasic was informed about continuing operations towards Zepa, and he says "leaving other work to the MUP," and it talks about removal of the remaining civilian population from Srebrenica. And at paragraph 2: "Killing of about 8.000 Muslim soldiers whom we blocked in the woods near Konjevic Polje. Fighting is going on. This job is being done solely by MUP units." Could you comment on this document and what is going on at the time on 13 July.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as in the evening of the 11th of July, when the first part of the column managed to make it across the road between Nova Kasaba and Konjevic Polje, on the evening of the 12th, large portions of the column they hadn't come across yet were also trying to cross the road, the difference, of course, being within the 24 hours that the Bosnian Serb military and police forces had been able to reinforce that area, and by the late evening hours of the 12th of July, the early morning hours of 13 jump, they were capturing at first hundreds and later that number escalated into thousands of prisoners that were then being detained at locations such as the Nova Kasaba football pitch, Konjevic Polje, Sandici, and other locations. So there was a -- throughout the morning hours, early morning hours of the 13th, a growing awareness of the prisoners that were being taken, the fact -- the size of the numbers of individuals who were still trapped behind the road and had not managed to escape towards the Zvornik zone. Now, Mr. Vasic is also being told by the army that the decision has been made that the army is going to pull out most of their mobile forces and begin military operations towards Zepa. So while he says that the entire job is now being done by the MUP, in fact there are still some army units that are participating, but the majority of the forces there, certainly from his perspective, would be MUP forces. So he's not totally inaccurate with that comment. But, you know, in its totality, it is General Vasic doing the same thing that he did the day before, which is being diligent in ensuring that his particular chain of command is informed not about -- not only about the military situation that is occurring but even reporting as to what decisions that the army has been taking and what the impacts will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just very briefly, I don't want you to speculate, but the -- in your view, the killing of the 8.000 Muslims, is that about some kind of crime or about combat or something else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I believe again I've testified to this particular issue. In the context on the 12th, the morning hours of the 12th or the morning hours of the 13th, the context that they're referring to is the operation against the column. They're viewing it as a military objective, and it's the fighting involved. It's not criminal activity per se.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your observation about the number, 8.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The general estimates of the size of the column tend to range anywhere from 10- to 15.000. And along the same vein, the general estimates of the part of the column that managed to cross the road successfully from the Bratunac area to the Zvornik area, most people generally refer to that as about a third of the column got through. So if you're using a 15.000 number or even low 10- or 12.000 number, that 8.000 number gives you that two-thirds. So obviously they weren't in there in direct contact with this column, and they were basing their number estimates off of interrogations of prisoners as they captured them, but it's not an unreasonable number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, back to you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we'll get to it when we talk to some documents -- with some documents specifically about the 16th and the opening of the corridor to let the column through by Vinko Pandurevic, but if you could just tell us briefly, at the beginning, was the VRS's -- or the Serb force -- Bosnian Serb forces' estimate of the column strength and the threat posed by it, did that evolve over time or did they have a clear understanding right from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did evolve over time. The intercepts, particularly that begin on the morning of the 12th, start to reflect reports by individuals who were up along the road the evening of the 11th, the morning of the 12th, where they're talking about seeing this massive number of soldiers, members of the column. They are seeing these people in positions that no one anticipated that they were going to be in. Those reports continue on through the 12th and through the 13th, and they start to be picked up by Major Obrenovic who is the Chief of Staff of the Zvornik Brigade who is reporting these large numbers. The disconnect within the context of the leadership of the Drina Corps and the Main Staff is that even though they're hearing some of these numbers, they do not accept that the number is as high as it is, and they do not accept the fact that the military threat posed by the column is as grave as it is. The views of the people on the ground facing the column and the military leadership of the VRS actually don't come into alignment until the 14th, when at that point even the Main Staff and the Drina Corps command realise the significant threat to Zvornik, or the Zvornik municipality, posed by the column in part because they had ignored reports from the field which had accurately stated this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I tender this, Your Honour, 1931.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4942, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I now have 65 ter number 23699.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at tab 72, which is in the second binder, Mr. Butler. Sorry you have to switch. This is a MUP report from 13 July. You'd spoke earlier about awareness of prisoners. That's what I want to focus on. We see some comment about that in paragraph 2, speaking of the night of the 12th to the 13th. Could you comment on this document and reporting on prisoner issues.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. At this particular juncture, the evening of the 12th, the morning of the 13th, the -- I believe this is RDB -- I'm sorry. Yeah, this is -- no. This is just -- I'm trying to figure out. This originates from the MUP and RDB third sector, so they're getting reports of prisoners being captured along the road. As we know from multiple sources of information that that process started in earnest the evening of the 12th, by the morning of the 13th, initially hundreds, and then as the day wore on rapidly, that number increased to thousands. We have intercepts which talk about later that day at various areas where they're designated for collection estimates from people on the ground that it's a thousand in each location. There is overhead imagery that has been available which will show clusters of hundreds of individuals at some of these locations as well. So as the day rolls on from, you know, the early morning hours of the 13th through the day, the number of prisoners in the custody of both the VRS forces and the MUP forces from Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, Sandici, and later towards Kravica, increases in a dramatic fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4943, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, let me just ask a follow-up to that. Speaking in general, based on your expertise, not necessarily specific to the situation here on the 13th, when armed forces, whether they're police or army or both, start hearing reports of hundreds, thousands of prisoners being taken, what does that implicate in terms of logistical needs in order to deal with those now thousands of or large numbers of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the context of the logistical support for those prisoners, I mean, you can go down almost each branch of the military to kind of get a feel for that. For example, for the security officials and military police officials, the concerns are going to be assigning the necessary soldiers or finding the necessary soldiers to ensure the safety and security of the prisoners, to guard these individuals. For those people in the rear services branch, there are going to be concerns related to where are we going to find the necessary resources for food, water for these prisoners? Many of the prisoners will be expected to have injuries or need other medical care, so where would those medical provisions come from? Ultimately there will be discussions that should take place as to how to get prisoners from those initial collection points which are exposed and vulnerable because there are still large numbers of Muslim troops from the column floating around in those areas to areas where they can be more easily guarded. And so when you're talking about a number of prisoners that's starting in the hundreds and rapidly spiraling into the thousands, it's dramatically increasing the difficulty of successfully accomplishing all of those military tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll look at a document later on that deals more with the numbers and what's going on with the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 23689, please. We'll start looking at a couple of intercepts now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is at your tab 73, Mr. Butler. And this is a short intercept, but again speaking about the communication and sharing of information issue, if you could tell us what we see here and I'll note it's handwritten at the top. It's from the Drina Corps command, but it's handwritten at the top: Tomo Kovac staff sent to Zvornik CJB public security centre and Bijeljina staff for information, and then we can see the distribution list of the original distribution from the Drina Corps which includes the MUP. If you could just comment on this document.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As General Tolimir indicated on the previous day, the radio intercept units of the VRS were being tasked to monitor the Bosnian Muslim communications coming from the column. This is a report on one of them. And not only is that information being shared to the various army correspondents, but it is being shared with the MUP. And the way that I read this, it has gone to the MUP headquarters, and then they're retransmitting it in whole down -- or at least making sure that the information contained in it has been sent down to the Zvornik CSB and the Bijeljina staff for their information. So continuing efforts by the intelligence people at all sides to ensure everyone has the appropriate situational awareness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm sorry I misspoke. I referred to this as an intercept. For the record, it's a report of an intercepted communication. And just briefly the description of the information that they're passing on of a member of the column establishing contact and saying: "Give me a reply. What the fuck do we do?" And then the remark: "The Turks are losing patience. They're seeking permission. Their batteries are running low." What does this tell us about the situation in the column?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation particularly in the front of the column, they're becoming more desperate for guidance from their military leadership at 2 corps as to how they should proceed. It's just simply not a question of the military column walking out and trying to penetrate the lines. There is good deal of military planning and execution that has to be done in order to make arrangements for other military units on the ABiH side to attack, to create openings in the lines. That requires a good deal of co-ordination. And what comes through in this particular vignette of an intercept is that the individuals who are leading the column from a military perspective still don't have an awareness as to what the plan is for them. Where are they supposed to go? When are they supposed to be there? What are their objectives in seeking to get out of what is then deep from behind enemy territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4944, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now I'll go to an intercept that's actually an intercept. 65 ter 31005, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is your tab 76, Mr. Butler. I'm skipping ahead a little bit. This is the 13th July at 17.30. I won't go through it all. There's quite a lot of information here, but could you comment on this document, about what it says about the knowledge and the fact of taking of prisoners, and if you can tell us what you -- what the three points are that Y refers to a little bit down in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at this intercept, I mean the first number that is thrown out is their awareness that there are roughly -- at this point in time at 17.30 hours on 13 July 1995, that there are at least 6.000 prisoners in the custody of either the army or the MUP along these various roads, and one of the correspondents talks about at each point roughly 1.500 to 2.000. As I discussed earlier, the main collection points were Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, Sandici, and of course at this time nearly a thousand individuals from -- who had been previously collected at Sandici had already been walked or moved south to the Kravica -- or not south, but further to the west where they were now in the Kravica warehouse. And of course at 17.30 hours, the Kravica warehouse massacre is just beginning at this juncture, although it's unlikely at this point the two correspondents know that. So this intercept provides a snapshot of at least the awareness of the various numbers of prisoners that are being -- falling in the custody of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At this time we can admit it in full?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We -- I'm in your hands. Or we can admit it as part of our large admission process which we will be doing shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I assume that this was already part of the intercept testimony, so I don't see any problem to fully admit it at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4945, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. If I could now have 30997, another intercept. This is one you're familiar with, I believe, Mr. Butler. It's at 19.45 on the 13th. X calling from General Krstic's looking for Ljubisa who has gone to Bratunac. And my first question will be -- well, I'll just ask you to tell us what -- what does this intercept say to you, and if you could remind us what "General Krstic's" would refer to at this point.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time on the 13th of July, General Krstic is back at the headquarters of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica, and this -- what happened shortly in a few minutes in this time, General Krstic will be promoted to become the commander of the Drina Corps. So in this context, it is somebody from the Drina Corps looking for Ljubisa Borovcanin, who at this time we're also aware has gone to Bratunac. So this is essentially somebody on behalf of General Krstic from the Drina Corps calling to make contact with Ljubisa Borovcanin in order to get a situation report as to what is happening, particularly asking questions, locations from Bijeljina, Janja, Doboj. Those refer to locations where police units have been dispatched to head south to the area in order to reinforce the military situation that's going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would tender this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why is it of seven pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's the various versions, Your Honour. I think from the printout, as well, in order to go back to the date. Otherwise, I'm not -- to be honest, I'm not sure exactly what we have in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While you're tendering only this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I would tender -- in fact, I won't tender it at this time, Your Honour. Let me consult. I'll put this together in the correct way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, this might seem like an odd question, but it's relevant for other evidence in this trial: As of the 13th of July, 1995, did General Krstic have any widely known physical disabilities or any physical handicaps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Earlier in the war, I believe November of 1994 or October of 1994, General Krstic stepped on a landmine while he was the commander of the Romanija Light -- or Romanija Motorised Brigade, and I believe he lost his -- he lost his foot. I'm not sure which side. At least I think close to his knee. So ultimately, he was medically sent back to Belgrade, had one of his -- foot and, you know, part of his leg amputated, received a prosthetic device, was brought back onto active duty again, and at that juncture this is where he assumed the role as the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps. So he was one of the few generals at least that I'm aware of at least in the VRS who had a disability like that and remained on active duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd now like to look at 31008A, another intercept from 13 July, this one from about roughly an hour later from the one we just looked at. And it's between General Krstic and Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what I'm interested in here is if you can tell us your analysis of the significance of this conversation, particularly in light of the events at Kravica which you discussed a minute ago having started that afternoon around 5.00 p.m. or so.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, in this context, General Krstic is now the corps commander. He is in this particular case reaching out to Mr. Borovcanin in order to get a situation report of the situation along the road where he knows that Borovcanin's police are located. General Krstic has driven that road earlier, so he has his own personal awareness of the situation, and he knows that Borovcanin is in command of the police forces there, so he's calling for a situation update. Now, on the side of Borovcanin, he was physically present at the Kravica warehouse as the massacre in part was occurring. So Borovcanin has the awareness of what is started and is continuing to some degree later in the night, and so when they're talking about the military situation, you know, Krstic is asking are there any problems? Borovcanin is telling him not only no problems militarily, as far as Borovcanin is concerned, you know, the fact that nearly a thousand individuals were massacred at the Kravica warehouse hasn't presented any problem that he thinks he needs to make General Krstic aware of either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- just a second, Mr. Butler. You stated that Mr. Borovcanin was physically present at the Kravica warehouse as the massacre in part was occurring. What is your basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I recall correctly from the various interviews of Mr. Borovcanin, I am aware of one interview where he states that after the beginning of the massacre when he received information that several the police to include one of the officers were wounded, he rushed down to the Kravica warehouse. He then took those officers, I believe Mr. Kudric [phoen] being one of them, to the Bratunac medical centre for treatment. So if Mr. Borovcanin's accounts of what he did when, he did it, and who he took to the medical centre are accurate in that reflect, it indicates that he would have been at the Kravica warehouse at the time the massacre was occurring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, I'm going to ask the Trial Chamber to disregard the information concerning Mr. Borovcanin's knowledge or participation in this massacre as beyond the witness's expertise and also by -- by eliciting evidence of what Mr. Borovcanin said in an interview with the OTP. I believe that crosses the line of proper expert testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, would you like to reply or just skip that part?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I would reply that a -- just briefly, Your Honour, that he, Mr. Butler, is interpreting this conversation, and I think he can rely on the whole of his knowledge that he's gained working in the case, and he -- he has reviewed that. I think the Chamber can assign this the correct way without striking any part of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What Mr. Butler stated in response to my question was from his interview with Borovcanin, not from his expertise as such. So I would like you to skip that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you one follow-up question on this. Are you aware of video shot by Mr. Pirocanac, Petrovic-Pirocanac, a journalist, while he was with Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The Petrovic video, as it is known, was filmed by a Belgrade news reporter. Much of the video that is described as the Petrovic video takes place, you know, on the 13th of July and covers going up and down that particular road. Now, on the 13th of July, Mr. Petrovic was in the car with Mr. Borovcanin. He was driving with him. That Petrovic video passes in front of the Kravica warehouse on the 13th of July at a point in time after the massacre started. So there is -- I mean, if we have to take it to that next step, if one assumes that Mr. Petrovic is still in the car with Mr. Borovcanin, and he is as far as I know, that's video corroboration of Borovcanin's own statement as to where he was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll move on now. Could I have P02987.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at your tab 159, Mr. Butler. This is Mr. Borovcanin's report of 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, say again, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Tab 159. Mr. Borovcanin's report of 13 July. Could you just take a look at this document, and again, tell us what it -- I'll ignore for the moment the part about Potocari, but if we look at page 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Nicholls. In the meantime, Mr. Robinson, do you object to the admission of the intercept between Borovcanin and Krstic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll admit that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4946, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, I'll ask you your -- to explain the notice issue and the logistics issue of Borovcanin's report that: "... we captured or had surrendered to us around 1.500 Muslim soldiers. The number increases by the hour."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, as I indicated earlier, there are a number of factors that commanders need to start considering with respect to the life support for numbers of prisoners of this nature. Again, he is using in this particular context the number of 1.500, and I'm not sure if there has ever been an exact time as assigned to when this report was drafted by Mr. Borovcanin, but even -- just even using that as a static number regardless of what point in time it is on the 13th of July, it's raising those same issues that Borovcanin like other military commanders needs to address: How do we secure these prisoners? Where do I get the forces to secure these prisoners? How do I provide them food, water, and medical support? How do I transport them from the initial location where they are currently being detained to more secure locations where they can not only be more easily guarded, but removed from where the effects of the battle-field would be more likely to occur, which would be on those road locations because there are still armed elements of the column seeking to cross the road. So these are the awareness issues that Mr. Borovcanin should have been considering whilst noting the fact that he has that number of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when we're speaking of this large number of prisoners and it says "increasing by the hour," Mr. Borovcanin is reporting it, but is that something that would normally, just keeping in mind that you've discussing how the army was now proceeding to Zepa for that stage of the campaign, is this information that needs to be dealt at the higher levels than the people on the road and in the brigades?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and particularly for the police. The police do not have their own logistical organs. They are entirely dependent upon the army for even supporting themselves. So in that vein, they are also now entirely dependent upon the army for supporting these number of prisoners since they don't have the resources to do that. And the numbers of prisoners that are being discussed in this context, I mean, when you look at them in light of the numbers of friendly forces, those Bosnian Serb police forces and VRS forces that are in those same areas, the number of prisoners that they are taking are outnumbering their own friendly forces. So that number in and of itself is setting up a security issue that certainly is beyond Mr. Borovcanin's issue or his control to deal with all by himself. So these are issues being raised that he needs support from his higher staffs at the police level as well as the army level.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I now have P04618.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That should be at your tab 78, Mr. Butler, going back. This is an intercept at 8.10 p.m. on the 13th of July, and it's between Miroslav Deronjic and President Karadzic via an intermediary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since we haven't received the redacted version, we'll not broadcast this. I was told that this is under seal. Probably because of some name which is appearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're correct, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a couple questions on this, Mr. Butler. We see at one point the intermediary says, "Deronjic, the president is asking how many thousands." And the answer is: "About two for the time being." And then the intermediary says, "Two, Mr. President." And Mr. Deronjic says, "But there will be more during the night." My only question on that is what is the situation in Bratunac around 8.00 p.m. regarding prisoners being held there? And just wait a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm going to object to the witness attempting to interpret this conversation between a civilian commissioner and President Karadzic. I don't believe that this is within his expertise. He can certainly answer this particular question as to what was going on in Bratunac at that time, but in terms of giving any comment or interpretation as a military expert to this conversation, I don't believe that it's within his expertise to do so and it would invade the province of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, if I can just respond, Your Honour. As Mr. Robinson said, this question wasn't objectionable and I was not going to ask Mr. Butler to interpret this conversation. However, if I did, I don't think it would invade your -- your sphere because, of course, you can always decide what to take and leave from the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So could you answer the question, please, Mr. Butler, just what's the situation in Bratunac at this time regarding prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this particular time, the able-bodied men who had been separated out on both the 12th and the 13th of July in Potocari have for the most part been transported and are being detained in a number of facilities in Bratunac. We refer to those facilities as -- the hangar is one of the first ones that they were detained in, later in the Vuk Karadzic school. So in that particular respect -- as well as a number of prisoners who had been earlier captured along the road and brought into Bratunac. So in that particular respect, the number that Mr. Deronjic notes of 2.000 is probably accurate. There's certainly other information out there that talks about the number of prisoners in Bratunac exceeding the number of soldiers and the police available to guard them to a point where many Bosnian Serb civilians who are of able body are being called forward and given weapons and being instructed to guard prisoners, because as the situation develops during the evening, there's very genuine fear that with prisoners outnumbering people to guard them, there could be a significant security situation in Bratunac. As the evening wears on, additional thousands of prisoners are brought in from places like Nova Kasaba and Konjevic Polje. So once the fixed facilities are full to capacity, many of those prisoners are -- remain stranded on buses and trucks, and they're parked at various locations where they can be more easily guarded, in some cases buses in front of the Vuk Karadzic school and other places. They are just left in buses and trucks at the Vihor transportation facility. So where Deronjic notes the fact that about 2.000 for the time being and notes that more will be coming in the evening is an accurate reflection of exactly the situation as it unfolds that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. This intercept is timed at 0810 hours. Are there any prisoner movements that take place from Bratunac on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My understanding is that the first convoy of prisoners from the Bratunac municipality to the Zvornik municipality leaves the hangar at approximately 2000 hours on 13 July and arrives at the school in Grbavci, which is associated with the Orahovac killing fields, approximately midnight on 13 July 1995, so they're there between 12.00 and 1.00 in the morning on the 14th of July. And that's the first convoy that I am aware of that leaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And based on your study, what was the knowledge of NGOs or international organisations about whether there were any prisoners in Bratunac during this period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly the Dutch had significant knowledge of this insomuch as there were many Dutch soldiers in Bratunac, and in fact the Dutch were still dealing with and with wounded Bosnian Muslims who were at various -- at least one facility in Bratunac. Along the same vein, there's additional information, some of it captured in the Petrovic video, of various international organisation relief convoys that are stopped at the international border at Ljubovija and even north, you know, across from Zvornik that are trying to get in there to provide relief to what they believe the humanitarian situation is with respect to Srebrenica and Potocari and are being blocked by the Republika Srpska authorities from crossing the river in part because once they cross the river through Bratunac, what is awaiting them in Bratunac cannot be hidden. They're going to see that scene and presumably report back to their superiors on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you know, when did those convoys gain access? Do you know when they began to come in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that sometime by the late afternoon of the 14th and I think they're rolling certainly on the 15th. So at some point on the 14th of July there was a decision to begin to allow some of these NGO convoys into the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm done with that. I now want to move on to 65 ter 2150, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is -- this is at your tab 17, Mr. Butler, in the -- I'm sorry, in the first binder. And this is headed -- it's from the Zvornik Brigade. It's headed "Delivery book Kp6." You refer to this in your revised narrative at footnote 381.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could have page 8 of the English, and I think it will be 116 of the Serbian. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you just tell us why did you note this in your report, and what does this log-book tell you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The log-book is simply a log of a general delivery vehicle that is employed in the -- by the Zvornik Brigade for general delivery purposes. Why I noted this in my particular report was that it is one of several documents which reflects the presence of police, and in this particular case military police, at a facility known as Orahovac. So as part of my doing analysis to understand the overall military situation in Grbavci and Orahovac and who was there based on the documents, this is one of the documents that I rely on that notes a police presence at Orahovac. When you look at the timing, this is the last entry related to the period of 13 July, and I think it's a little bit clearer on the Serbo-Croatian version, because it notes 0100. So I take that as 0100 on 14 July, which corresponds with my understanding of when the military police roughly arrived, as well as when the first bus convoys from Bratunac arrived in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I -- do you have a question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm just wondering what part is being tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would tender just the pages for 13 July and the cover sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that's -- very well. I have no problem admitting that. The cover page and the sheet for 13th of July, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just briefly let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just clarify something. Is it the whole page where it says the 13th -- where the says the 13th, or should the entry where it says the 14th of July also be included?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit this page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, could the translation be revised again, because under the 14th, it refers to a funeral vehicle. Loznica-Sekovic, and then it refers to a funeral vehicle, which doesn't appear in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I will send it for a revised translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we give the number for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4947, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One follow-up question. You explained it quite well, but just to make it clear, how -- how do you arrive at the conclusion that this is military police rather than regular or MUP police being referred to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in part it's constructive analysis because one of the other documents that I have reviewed is the military police roster for the Zvornik Infantry Brigade for July of 1995, and on that particular document - and I think we're going to get to it at some juncture - there were notations on that document that reflected a number of military police at Orahovac on the 14th of July. Those were subsequently altered at some juncture in an effort by somebody to hide the fact that a number of military police people were in Orahovac on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In that case, let's -- let's bring that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's 65 ter 2211.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's at your tab 19, Mr. Butler. And if we go to -- this is a little bit difficult to go through and I don't want to spent a long time on it, but can you just tell us: Is this the document you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, unfortunately the English translation we have doesn't include all the headings, but if we go to -- if I could have one moment. Well, if we could go to, for example, entry 37, which should be on page 3, I think, of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, really, simply in the interests of time, is this a document that you were referring to that had Os and Rs erased and replaced with Ts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we need the English translation at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. I agree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, actually this is fine right here. We have Stanoje Bireakovic [phoen] as number 17, and if we look across at the dates for 14th and 15th, we see these large Ts written in. Is that one of the entries you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe what I have done as a component of my report is I listed the names of the individuals who had the corresponding eraser marks from this document in my report and noted whether they had either an O or an R next to their name and on what corresponding date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'll note, Your Honours, that can be found in the Srebrenica narratives at footnotes 370, 372, 373, 379, 394, and 396, discussions of this issue. And also I do have the original if any party wishes to see it. It's very clear on the original. May I tender that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4948, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence would like to have the original, because we're not certain that an unequivocal conclusion can be drawn on these deletions. Only a handwriting expert, a graphologist, could establish this. To say -- to be quite frank, I don't see that anything has been deleted on this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have the copy, and perhaps during the break or I can give it to Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What Mr. Karadzic said was that he wanted to see an original of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I have the original in the courtroom, which in my submission would be you don't need any expert analysis to see that there's been some erasures and written over, but my submission would be it's quite clear on the original log seized from the Zvornik Brigade which I can provide to him to review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I now have P04464.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at your tab 86, Mr. Butler. This is the Main Staff report to President Karadzic from 13 July. If we could go to page 3 of the English as well as the Serbian original. I'd like you to comment on the information receiving President Karadzic in the report for 13 July regarding the Drina Corps zone. We see it under number 6.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially subparagraph (a) talks about the general military situation, specifically noting that the enemy from the former enclave of Srebrenica are in a state of total disarray. Troops are surrendering in large numbers to the VRS. It also notes in the next sentence a 200- to 300-strong group of soldiers managed to make it through the sector at Mount Udrc and are trying to break through to the territory under Muslim control. As I noted in some of my earlier testimony, this is where you see this disconnect between what the people on the ground believed to be much larger numbers of individuals who broke through as the first part of a column versus what is actually being acknowledged and reported up to the higher level. They just, frankly, don't believe the numbers that they're hearing as to the threat of the column or the size of the column at this juncture, and of course by discounting those numbers, that leads to the military threat that occurs starting the 14th and 15th and 16th of July. It also notes the situation in the corps under subparagraph (b), that various military units are engaged in scouring the terrain of the municipality, and also talks about the fact that other corps units are in the final stages of -- for preparations to begin, or as they say here, settle the issue at Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. That's the last document, I think, now, from the 13th of July. Moving on to the 14th, events of that day, which we already began talking about with Orahovac in the early hours of the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 4057.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at your tab 90, Mr. Butler. This is a 14 July report from the Zvornik chief, Vasic, up to the RS minister of the MUP and his Bijeljina centre. What I'd like you to talk about is the areas of combat that they talk about in paragraph 1, and then the paragraph after paragraph 8, which talks about, again, large numbers of enemy soldiers surrendering.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. To belabour the point, just like he was doing on the 12th and the 13th of July, on the 14th Mr. Vasic is still, to the best of his ability, diligently reporting on the situation as he is aware of it to his higher headquarters. He talks about the general military situation, where enemy forces are believed to be and what combat has occurred. The -- the size of the enemy column which he talks about is 3 kilometres through the day. He talks about the specific tasks that each of the PJP companies under his control are engaged in, as well as what the task of some of the other PJP companies that have come into the area are doing. He notes that during combat operations the previous day, which would be 13 July, the enemy suffered serious losses in manpower, and again notes the phrase "larger numbers of enemy soldiers surrendered to our units."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in the top paragraph speaking of the areas of combat, main combat activities in the general areas of Sandici, Bratunac municipality, Konjevic Polje, et cetera, would Kravica be in that same general area? Combat was thought to have occurred there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kravica is in the same general area, but there was no combat operations occurring at Kravica on any of those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I tender this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4949, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Could I have 31050, and I think C is the best one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is at your tab 92, Mr. Butler. It's an intercept between Palma, which is Zvornik; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Duty officer Major Jokic, and Badem, which is Bratunac; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you just again remind us, we're now on the 14th of July at 9.00 p.m., when it refers to Palma duty officer Major Jokic, who is that in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Jokic by position is the engineering officer of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. He is also performing the functions as the brigade duty officer in the duty operations centre on 14 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We are not to broadcast this. As far as the original is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I think the translation may be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we can see from this intercept that on the 14th of July at this time, Beara is in Bratunac, Major Jokic is calling from Zvornik. First when we see it down the page -- I'll try to go through this quite quickly. Major Jokic says, "We were together, Colonel, sir, number 155 called you and asked you to call him urgently." What extension is 155?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that extension 155 is the phone line that is in the operations centre of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm not going to ask you to say what Major Jokic means exactly, but Jokic says, "Yes, hey, we have huge problems over here. There are big problems, well, with the people -- I mean with the parcel." And then he says, "Drago is nowhere around." And earlier on he says that it's urgent that he talk to Beara. So the question is: At 9.00 p.m. in Zvornik, what is the situation for the Zvornik Brigade? What is going on that -- that could be considered urgent?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular context, by 9.00 p.m. on the 14th of July, there -- you know, from a military perspective, the column has already broken through the initial ambush positions of the Zvornik Brigade that were set previously that day and is now believed to be working its way towards the north-west, towards what they would call free territory, but the brigade has no real contact with them because they've got no forces in that area at the time. From the perspective of prisoners who had been brought into the Zvornik Brigade zone, at that particular time the prisoners who had previously been brought and were held at the Grbavci school are still being executed in Orahovac. I don't believe that those executions are concluded until midnight on the 14th of July, 1995. You have roughly a thousand prisoners who are already in the old school at Petkovci. You have prisoners that are in the school at Rocevic, and you have prisoners being brought up to the school facility at Pilica. I don't believe at this juncture they've reached that overflow point at Pilica where they're putting them in the Dom of Culture yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you say the school at Grbavci is that the same as the school at Orahovac associated with the Orahovac execution site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Your Honour, this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is also part of a bunch of exhibits which have been, so to speak, authenticated by the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. Robinson. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We'll put it under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I -- yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4950, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I would like you to produce a redacted version later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, of course. I think this would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What you're going to do is replace the original one with the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think -- yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't need to give a separate --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- exhibit number. Unless Defence has any objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we don't, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you could go to tab 94, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is 31072, and that is the 65 ter number. It is an intercept. Your Honour, I think we can broadcast the English completely although, unfortunately, the B/C/S still has names on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Still on the 14 July, Mr. Butler, this intercept's at 22.27, and it states it's between General Vilotic and Jokic who we just talked about, who Jokic is. There are again discussions of problems in the field blocking the large group coming towards the asphalt and it being blocked, where are the blues. And first of all, can you tell us who you think the General Vilotic referred to is here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe in this particular context General Vilotic as referred here is, in fact, General Miletic, who is the Chief of Operations for the VRS Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. How do you arrive at that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first thing is there is no General Vilotic in either the VRS or, as far as we checked, within the VJ forces. It sounds -- I mean, and clearly there is a General Miletic who is with the Main Staff of the VRS. So potentially a slightly garbled identification of the name. Clearly Major Jokic knows who he's talking to. So it only makes sense in that regard that it could be General Miletic or that it is, in fact, General Miletic who is having this discussion with the duty officer of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And what about the line where Jokic says: "Understood" -- starts to say "Col" and then says, "General, sir"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milovanovic was one of the number of generals who had been recently promoted I believe in June of 1995, either late May or early June 1995. So it would make sense that Major Jokic would have made that type of a slip still referring to him back as his former rank since he had only been a general for probably less than 60 days at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, did you mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, speaking of slips. Milovanovic or Miletic --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got generals on the brain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you just tell me, please, then, your knowledge of the situation in Zvornik, what this is about, specifically where Vilotic or, you believe, Miletic says, We'll see about it with that Vasic, everything available should be gathered. You must raise them all, Jokic, sound the alert down in the town. Everyone who can carry a rifle should go up." What's going on at that time in Zvornik? You've already talked about that a bit.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again talking about that from before, we're now at a point chronologically in time with respect to the Srebrenica operation that the highest levels of the VRS now understand the threat that the column poses to the Zvornik municipality in general and the Zvornik Infantry Brigade in particular. Vasic is the head of the CSB, and you know, in this particular issue he's talking about, you know, make sure that Vasic understands this. The implied task is that, you know, Vasic needs to bring more police in or reallocate his police forces to be able to assist in the combat operations. The fact -- raising the alert, ensure all units are fully mobilised. Anyone who can carry a rifle needs to be at the defensive positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And then there's a section about -- a little bit below: "Obrenovic is really engaged to the maximum. We are all, believe me. This packet has done the most to ruin us. We've been reporting on the number of people, well, so --" And the general of the Main Staff says, "Okay, don't talk to me about that." Again, since this is 14th July, evening hours, around 10.30, this is when there were executions continuing at Orahovac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is also part of intercept that were authenticated. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4951, provisionally under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The reason why we should put this under seal is because of initial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. And we need to redact and come up with a copy that doesn't have the names that we've -- it's been the practice not to broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you could go to tab 95, Mr. Butler. This is the last document from the 14th of July that I want to look at. P04457. This is the Main Staff report to the president, dated 14 July, which again covers all the different corps but I want to look at the Drina Corps, number 6, which is on page 3 of both English and Serbian, and ask you to comment on section 6(b).

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. With respect to 6(b), another of the accumulating comments speaking about although not in a numerical form, even at this point on the 14th they are scouring the terrain and receiving a large number of Muslim fugitives who are surrendering to them. So they're still reporting on, although unspecified, large numbers of Muslims who are surrendering to the military and the police forces that are operating in the Milici, and Bratunac and Skelani Brigade areas in the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again this very urgent report of 14 July doesn't go just to the president but to the commands of all the corps; is that right? And the various IKMs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That was the custom. Not only did you keep your superior informed, in this context the president of the Republika Srpska, it was also sent to all of the corps commands as well. So the senior leadership of the army had a broad situational awareness as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now moving on to the 15th of July. I'll try to move quickly through some relevant documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have 31091A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at your tab 96, Mr. Butler. I'm going to look now at a -- at just a couple of intercepts which mention Colonel Beara. And this one, 15 July, in the morning, 0952, Colonel Beara looking for General Zivanovic, he was to call him at 139. What is 139? Which extension is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Extension 139 is the phone extension for the security office of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. It is what we refer to as -- that is Drago Nikolic's phone number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And so where, based on your analysis and all the documentation, is Colonel Beara that morning on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning he is at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would tender that, Your Honour, which I -- it's complicated. I think this one does not need to be under seal from what I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I see a signature --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Actually, it should be, yeah. I was looking at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4952, provisionally under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. If you could go to tab 97 now, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if I could have 31096C.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is just a short while later in the morning on 15 July. It's 9.54 now, a couple minutes later. And it's General Zivanovic and Colonel Beara, who we saw mentioned in the previous intercept. I won't go through this -- this entire document, but can you tell me what this is about based on the situation at the time faced by the VRS and MUP that morning?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular intercept, particularly when you couple it with an intercept that comes several minutes later, reflects a conversation between General Zivanovic and Colonel Beara relating to the failure of one of the brigade commanders, Colonel Furtula, Lieutenant-Colonel Furtula, to send soldiers from his particular unit to a specified location in accordance with the boss's orders. This particular part of the conversation is somewhat cryptic, but it reflects that both General Zivanovic and Colonel Beara at least understand what the boss's orders are in this particular context, and that instead of having a platoon of the roughly 60 men, he has only two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And which brigade did Furtula -- which was his brigade, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: His brigade was the Visegrad Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And that's a mention of Lukic is waiting at Blagoje -- is waiting at Blagojevic and "Lukic is here with me." Do you have any insight from your research on who this Lukic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where is he from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Lukic is from Visegrad. At this particular point in time he was a subordinate -- one of the subordinate unit commanders in the Visegrad Brigade, and various individuals have talked about the fact that him and his unit had been ordered to come up in part to participate in executions of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, at one point Beara says, "Have him send at least half," and I won't go through it all, and Zivanovic says, "I can't order that anymore." Why can't -- why is it on the 15th that Zivanovic can't order something anymore?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Zivanovic, while still being a general in the VRS, is no longer at this point in time the commander of the Drina Corps. So what he is doing, you know, quite properly from a military command context, is letting, you know, Colonel Beara know that, you know, I'm no longer authorised to give those commands. And if you read further into this particular intercept, he provides Colonel Beara the extension number to call for the person who could, in fact, give those orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you just point us to that in the -- in the intercept.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of the first page he talks about telephone exchange 385.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it states "Zlatar," and again Zlatar is which unit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zlatar is the telephonic code-name used by the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I would tender this intercept which would need to be under seal at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. That will be admitted as Exhibit P4953, provisionally under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you go to the next tab, Mr. Butler, and if I could have 31086. Again in this series of conversations featuring Colonel Beara, we now have an intercept at 10.00 in the morning between General -- between Colonel Beara and General Krstic, now that Colonel Beara has gotten the direction from Zivanovic. And the first thing I'll ask you is who is Boban Indjic, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that Boban Indic is again also from the Visegrad area, and at this point in time he is a deputy to Milan Lukic.
