utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you just tell us, again based on the previous intercepts and the situation on 15 July, military, what's going on in the Zvornik Brigade area, what is this conversation about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, militarily in the Zvornik Brigade area, the column is continuing to move to the north-west, starting to make preparations for what would later be an attack to try and break through the lines. This particular conversation, however, has nothing to do with the overall military situation. This particular conversation has to do with the fact that on the 15th of July, or I should say more accurately continuing on the 15th of July, they're engaged in executing thousands of prisoners and that they are having difficulty getting enough individuals to participate in order to get all of these prisoners killed within whatever the required time-frame is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, when we see here Krstic says, "I'll see what I can do," as Beara is asking for men, Beara says, "Check it out and have him go to Drago's." What would that be a reference to? It's about a little over halfway down the first page.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this particular context with Beara saying, "Have them go to Drago's," he's basically directing that they go to Drago Nikolic's or report to Drago Nikolic who is the security officer of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, and that is where Beara is right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when Krstic says, "Ljubo, then take those MUP guys from up there," and Beara says, "No, they won't do anything. I talked to them and there's no other solution but for those 15 to 30 men with Indjic that were supposed to arrive on the 13th but didn't." Do you have any more information about - and it's in your report as well, I believe - the failure of a group of men to arrive at this time in the area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My understanding and from the documents that I've been able to look at, it's not a question of Furtula deliberately not following the order. There is, I believe, an intercept which discusses the fact that the bus that these individuals were travelling on broke down, so it was as a result of a mechanical issue why these particular soldiers did not or were not able to arrive to do the jobs that they were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally at the bottom Beara is saying, "I don't know what to do. I mean it, Krle. There are still 3,500 parcels," and the operatives put it in quotes, "that I have to distribute and I have no solution." I'm not asking you to say what he meant by that, but the morning the 15th of July, 1995, what is the situation in regards to prisoners being held in schools in the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the morning of the 15th, Colonel Beara, particularly being in Zvornik, should be aware that the prisoners are already being killed at both Orahovac and at the Petkovci school. He is aware that there are still prisoners at the Rocevic school, there are prisoners at Pilica, and there are -- at this point in time they'll be putting prisoners who can't fit into the school at Pilica into the Dom of Culture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Also in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Also under seal provisionally?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4954, provisionally under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P00108, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to go through this quite quickly. This is referred to in footnote 414 -- excuse me, 399 and 412, and actually quite a few places in your narrative. It's the -- it's a daily orders log entry for 15/16 July of the Zvornik Brigade Engineering Company. Could you just tell us why you included this in your report and what its significance was to you. It's -- I'm sorry, it's at tab 99.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got it. Yes, I've got it. The -- the forensics of the investigation as well as witness testimony from survivors outlines locations of where the initial mass graves were. One of the investigative questions pursued was who was responsible for burying the bodies of the individuals. This particular document from the Engineer Company of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade reflects equipment at locations on the 15th of July in Orahovac and Petkovci which could only be engaged in that activity, and the fact that they are listed in the orders book, the daily orders book for the Engineer Company reflects in my mind the fact that they're operating there under military control. So in fact it is member of -- it is members of the Engineer Company who are engaged in burying those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a quick follow-up. Why do you say that's the only activity that they could be engaged in at these places on those dates?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from a military perspective, there is no combat activity occurring at the location of Orahovac or Petkovci on those dates. Both of those locations are far from the front lines, and there is no logical reason for that equipment to be working there for a military purpose, i.e., digging defensive positions or things of that nature. So once you exclude all of those things out and corresponding to where the locations of the mass graves are, it leaves you the only logical conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go to P00138.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at tab 101, Mr. Butler. This is Vinko Pandurevic's interim combat report from 15 July. It's got a lot of information in it. You cite this - I won't go through all the footnotes - quite heavily in your narrative. Could you just tell us the significance of this document. If you could just quickly go through it for us.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, starting from the back, perhaps, and moving forward for an appreciation, you can see that there is a sent stamp on this particular document of 15 July 1995 at 1925 hours. So it reflects the awareness of the brigade and specifically in this case with the signature of the brigade commander on the original B/C/S version of that. The -- the awareness of the brigade commander, Colonel Pandurevic, at or before this particular time when this report is sent, that part is important because it has to be realised that Colonel Pandurevic, when the day began on the 15th of July, was with his forces in the Zepa enclave, and only in the early morning hours of the 15th, I think somewhere around the line of 8.00 or 9.00, those forces were disengaged and Colonel Pandurevic was directed to return to the Zvornik Brigade area in order to deal with the military situation. So Colonel Pandurevic is now coming into the brigade zone for the first time since he's left it on the 4th of July, I believe. So while he generally has an awareness of what's going on, this particular document by him reflects the detailed understanding he has of the situation throughout his brigade at this time. So the first paragraph discusses his understanding of the column and talks about, you know, 3.000 armed and unarmed enemy soldiers. It gives you an appreciation of the gravity of the threat of the column that Colonel Pandurevic recognises, as well as noting that the brigade forces are sealing off and searching the area and that several hundred -- few hundred is the word he uses, have already been killed, and those would be enemy soldiers from the column. It gives, the next paragraph, his appreciation of the situation from the 2 Corps and what he believes that the 2 Corps is doing in order to attempt to link up with the column and where he believes that main attack is coming from. It talks about, in the third paragraph, other military-related events that are occurring in the -- in the brigade zone, which would include artillery attacks. It would -- other smaller attacks. It notes his awareness of what his casualties are at that time, which are -- at least is reported four dead and a dozen or so wounded. And continuing on in that paragraph, again noting that they're sealing off various areas and that ultimately all the brigade forces are engaged and they have no reserve forces. The next paragraph is where Colonel Pandurevic notes his awareness of the prisoners that are in the Zvornik Brigade zone. He notes that: "An additional burden for us is the large number of prisoners distributed throughout schools in the brigade area, as well as obligations of security and restoration of the terrain," which in the Serbo-Croatian language translates as "asanacija." In this particular context, what he's talking about is an awareness, in my opinion, of the number of prisoners in the school, the security obligations at a minimum related to guarding them, and further, I believe the knowledge that they're being executed. And at the last part of the phrase, the "asanacija," an awareness that Zvornik Brigade military formations are being used to bury the bodies. The next paragraph talks about the command can no longer take care of these problems any longer, and it is neither the material or resources, and further notes: "If no one takes on this responsibility, I will be forced to let them go." In previous testimony I have been asked whether I believe in that context of letting them go, whether we're referring to the prisoners or the column. My answer was at that time and remains that in the context of where this particular statement is, I believe that Colonel Pandurevic is referring to the prisoners in the schools that he would be prepared to let go, not the column. The next paragraph is that he notes that he has been in some communication with his opposite number in the 2nd Corps, where he talks about making an offer on the other side to separate out civilians and have others surrender, but that his opposite number, the 28th Infantry -- the 24th Infantry Division person he's discussing this with has refused and they want the entire column to be released or let go. His last -- or his next sentence, "The situation is complicated but still under control," and at this particular point in time, he's correct. It is complicated but it is still under control. A lot of the major combat which occurs has yet to happen during the late evening hours of the 15th and the early morning hours of 16 July 1995. And he ends his report with a request once again reiterating his previous requests for additional reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in line with this report that we see talks about a large number of prisoners, I'd like to go to P04460.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's your tab 102. The same day, the Main Staff again report to the president. And again if we could look at page 3, the Drina Corps zone. And I just want to get your comment again about the reporting chain up through these various bodies which we see here in the report to the president, specifically as it refers to the situation in the former Srebrenica enclave and prisoners.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It discusses, again, as part of the column, the remainder of scattered Muslim formations from the former Srebrenica enclave are moving towards Kravica and Konjevic Polje. It talks about several enemy groups having surrendered to VRS members and then starts going into the situation related to Zvornik. So as in other days, there are reports going up by the Main Staff to the president of the republic as well as the other corps commands noting that the Drina Corps units are still capturing prisoners on these days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. With that, I'd like to now move to the 16th of July and go through some documents concerning the situation on that day, again speaking about the military situation in the Zvornik area -- Zvornik Brigade area and the situation with the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 31128A. Excuse me one moment. Yes, 31128A, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which is at your tab 103, Mr. Butler. This is a conversation on 16 July 1995 at 11.11 in the morning, between Colonel Beara and Cerovic. Do you know who Cerovic would be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is Colonel Cerovic, who is the assistant commander for morale, legal, and religious affairs at the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the conversation concerns something called triage to be done on the prisoners, and Beara comes on the line and speaks with Cerovic. And Cerovic eventually says, "So he told me he got instructions from above, yes, to do triage on those." And Beara says, "I don't want to talk about it on the phone." What I want to ask you is: On the 16th of July, having looked through logs of the Zvornik Brigade for vehicle logs, rear services logs, hospital logs, the type of material you said would need to be mobilised quickly when thousands of prisoners are taken in order to feed them, care for their medical needs, transport them to other exchange centres, things of that nature, did you find any documents supporting triage of that nature on the 16th of July in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The only references related to anything that could be medically remotely related to Zvornik and prisoners on 16th July is related to the prisoners who were -- wounded prisoners who started in Milici, were moved to the Zvornik medical centre, and ultimately from there moved to the Standard facility. That numbered at -- was a total of 13 prisoners. So in this particular context where you're talking about triage over a thousand prisoners, there are no documents or anything else that even would potentially relate to that as a medical context.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What is, if you know, Beara's involvement with prisoners on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Beara's involvement is related to the execution of the prisoners at Pilica and Dom of Culture and Branjevo on that day, and in fact, there are documents that will reflect -- both documents and intercepts reflect having to deal with particular logistics issues that will come up due to a lack of fuel in order to complete the full executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. We will get to some of those in a moment. And just if I can ask you again, it mentions, "Trkulja was here just with me -- was here with me just now -- was looking for you." Can you tell us who Trkulja is again?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Trkulja is an operations officer from the Main Staff. He's -- by position he's technically the chief of armour services. In this particular context where Cerovic is talking about "Trkulja being here with me looking for you," Cerovic is at the Drina Corps headquarters. So he's referring to the fact that Colonel Trkulja was physically at the Drina Corps headquarters looking for Beara, assuming that he might be there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I tender that provisionally under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4955, provisionally under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now simply to save time I won't bring it up, but can you recall whether there was an entry in the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook for 16 July, stating that it was reported from Zlatar that triage of wounded and prisoners must be carried out? It was reported to Beara. If you don't remember that, I can bring it up.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I've testified that in previous cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It has been already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just didn't -- I was trying to -- not to bring it up again. Could I have 65 ter 31143, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is at your tab 106, Mr. Butler. This is a brief intercept. If you could just tell me what this is about. It's between Zlatar, which we now know is Drina Corps, and Palma, Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular context, they're looking for -- Zlatar's asking: "Give me the 01." Normally when you hear intercept conversations like this, the 01 refers to the commander. In this particular case it notes that the commander is listening but they can't make a direct link, and Zlatar is asking, you know, give -- just have him brief me on what's knew for Zlatar 1. In this particular context, the communications or operations people are saying what does Colonel Pandurevic have for General Krstic so he's aware of the situation. And Palma is saying, "We made a small corridor so the civilians could pull out." And their words are illegible there. And then Zlatar says, "Nothing. Good luck and good-bye to you," and so that ends the conversation essentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And we see the time, it's 13.55. Is that significant for what's going on on the 16th with the column?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As I -- there's been a good deal of information that discusses this. Sometime in the early afternoon of the 16th of July and times vary between roughly, you know, 1.00 to maybe as late as 3.00 or 4.00. Colonel Pandurevic talking with his counterpart in the 28th -- or the 24th Division concluded a temporary battle-field truce which would allow for the column to depart the territory of the Republika Srpska and head towards what the Bosnian Muslims consider friendly lines. There were -- as I noted earlier, there were drastic changes in the military situation in the Zvornik Brigade from the 19.25 interim report that Colonel Pandurevic drafted on the 15th to what is now happening on the afternoon of the 16th. Many of those Colonel Pandurevic will actually lay out himself in his interim combat report, but there was a significant amount of combat, a number of VRS positions to include the 4th Infantry Battalion's command posts were overrun by the column, and in light of the rapidly deteriorating military situation, Colonel Pandurevic made a determination that he needed to allow the column to go through, that there was no point in attacking it anymore for the -- for the military gain that he was receiving or he was getting, which was now minimal at best.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I tender that, Your Honour. It would need to be provisionally under seal. Or perhaps the version we have up there is fine, actually. Sorry, I was looking at a different one in my ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it's of six pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh. I withdraw it. I'll -- I'll tender it separately later, Your Honour, if it's not in complete order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me just check it. But English is of three pages, and B/C/S is of six pages. Yes. If you could tender it --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll fix that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- after tidying it up. Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you go to tab 110, Mr. Butler. This is D02002. And we'll look at a couple of intercepts now, not directly in chronological order. This one is between the Main Staff and General Mladic, although General Mladic cannot be heard. To save time I won't go through it all, but the Main Staff office -- duty officer says: "Good day, General, sir, well, it's like this. I just sent a telegram to Toso while the president called a short while ago and said that he had been informed by Karisik that Pandurevic had arranged passage for the Muslims over to that territory," and then he continues talking about not having communication with Pandurevic. Can you just tell us what this intercept is about in relation to the situation in Zvornik you've just been describing and what it tells us about General -- President Karadzic's ability to communicate with the Main Staff and receive information through the MUP about army developments, military developments?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, first off, just as in previous cases, President Karadzic, when significant issues that affected the state came up, was not particularly shy about picking up the phone and directly trying to call the Main Staff or others in order to ascertain what was happening and what the impacts would be. At its face, this document reflects the fact that they're aware that President Karadzic has been calling down, asking information about this, and also noting that he's receiving information on this situation from Karisik, who is the head of the MUP -- or of the police forces of the MUP at this time. So in the sense that where I've discussed previously the multiple reporting chains that were existing and reporting all the way back up to the chain of command, this is an excellent opportunity of even though -- to demonstrate that even though President Karadzic is not receiving information about this yet from the military, he has an entirely different chain of information in reporting from the MUP side that he is hearing about this information. So he is well informed as to what is going on, and at this juncture asking the army to clarify and to provide additional information. Clearly he's caught the army by surprise, because even though General Krstic may be aware of Pandurevic's decision to open the column, as noted in the previous intercept, the Main Staff still hasn't been fully apprised of what is happening and is caught a little bit flatfooted as they're now trying to deal with answering the request from the president about this and their own subordinate military formation hasn't yet informed them of what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go quickly now then to 31120.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at your tab 109, Mr. Butler, before. As I said, we're going a bit out of order, because the intercept we just looked at was at 16.15 on the 16th, and now we're looking at one at 15.29 from the Main Staff to Palma, Zvornik Brigade. And could you just tell us how this intercept, the information here fits in to what you've just been discussing with us about this information on the corridor being opened?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What this particular document is related to the Main Staff in Palma is that they're also hearing information and receiving it -- like I said, they make it a point that they didn't get any information from the MUP, but they -- they got it from this other individual, from Novi Karakaj, and what they want is they want to hear from Colonel Pandurevic what is going on. They want him to dictate a report as to what is happening and send it to the Main Staff as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let me -- this is going slightly out of order, but if I could have 65 ter 31139, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at your tab 107. Still on 16 July at 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were you minded to tender that into --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I apologise. It has been -- no, it was not. I'm sorry. Yes, I do intend to tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I don't have any objection. I noticed that this intercept and a few others seem to have two copies of the same intercept and the same 65 ter number. I'm wondering if there's a particular reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The reason is, Your Honour, and Mr. Robinson, is -- I believe these have been put together to show the intercept from the different versions we have, from the notebook and from the printout. That's why there are two. And because they are sometimes, as we've seen in the testimony here, slightly different, and with the printout and the original, it is easily to roll back and see the date sometimes from the notebook. So it may be a little bit messy and we'll clean it up, but that is the idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that should be put provisionally under seal, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4956, provisionally under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, 31139 at your tab 107, Mr. Butler, the Chamber has actually seen this intercept before and seen the fuel log which we say is related to it and the duty officer notebook entry related to it with a different witness so I don't want to go through all that, but what I would like you to explain to us is on the 16th of July in the afternoon, what is -- you referred to this earlier. What is Colonel Popovic involved in where he needs 500 litres of D2 diesel fuel doing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like Colonel Beara, at this time Colonel Popovic, who was the chief of security for the Drina Corps, is up in the Pilica area, and they are dealing with the issues of the transportation of the prisoners from Pilica to Branjevo and their execution, and so as part of that process, you know, Colonel Popovic is having to deal with the issue of a lack of fuel for the transports of the prisoners from the Pilica school to Branjevo, and this whole chain of events noting all of the people who have to be called and who are ultimately involved in requisitioning the fuel through the proper sources so it could be used for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And as you say, requisitioning the fuel through proper sources. Forgetting for the moment that this fuel is being used to assist in a -- what we say is a murder operation, is the way the fuel is obtained, as we see in these intercepts and the fuel log, according to the way fuel would be attained for any military operation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I tender this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4957, provisionally under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, that was an intercept with Mr. Popovic on the 16th at around 2.00 p.m. I want to look now at 31145A. That's at your tab 111, Mr. Butler. 16th of July still, 16.43 now. Duty officer from Zlatar is calling, looking for Popovic, and says, "Listen, the boss wants one to -- of the two of them to Vinko to see what's going on." Speaking of Popovic or Drago Nikolic, to see what's going there. What is this about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the context of what's happening in Zvornik, you know, first is Zlatar duty officer referring to his boss. His boss is General Krstic, the corps commander. So he wants either his chief of security, Popovic, or Drago Nikolic, the Zvornik Brigade chief of security, to go to where Colonel Pandurevic is, which is -- at this point in time Colonel Pandurevic is at the brigade forward command post and getting report as to what is going on with respect to the column. For whatever reason, at this juncture still nobody has heard from Colonel Pandurevic as to the circumstances surrounding, first, the column and, second, what motivated his decision to authorise the column to pass through the lines as well as whatever else with respect to the broader situation related to the Zvornik military. So people are frantically trying to instruct others: Go to Colonel Popovic. Find out what's going on and report back. I'm sorry, Colonel Pandurevic, and report back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4958, provisionally under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, two more documents on this same topic. If I could have P00180.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, this should be one of two documents you have in tab 112. It's Vinko Pandurevic's interim combat report from 16 July 1995. And if you can briefly link up this interim combat report Pandurevic is sending to the topic we're going through at the moment.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, finally at this juncture and depending on whether you look at the date stamp of the report as in 1810 hours or 2000 hours, I mean somewhere between 6.00 and 8.00 p.m. on the 16th of July, Colonel Pandurevic's interim report about the situation finally gets sent to the Drina Corps headquarters where it lays out Colonel Pandurevic's assessment of the overall situation. He talks about the attacks that started at 0400 hours right where he predicted they would be, the 4th, 7th and 6th Infantry Battalion areas. Notes that the 4th Battalion was completely surrounded, and as he says in his column -- or in his number, counting the soldiers and civilians, armed and unarmed, I mean, they were surrounded by over 7.000 people. Talks about the viciousness or ferocity of the attack and noting that part of their -- not only part of the brigade forces are surrounded at Baljkovica, but that the enemy has suffered major losses and notes hundreds of dead. But even in fact -- even despite the casualties that they are incurring, they are still pushing out towards the north-west in order to break through. It notes what their forces are doing in paragraph 2. What the friendly situation is. Notes the dozens of wounded, ten dead, five missing in action, and also reflects the fact that he doesn't even have full reporting yet, that there are additional reports that will be sent, and that he's having difficulties getting his supplies and evacuating the wounded because the main road into that area has been cut off. Paragraph 3, imparting -- he's venting his frustration about the fact that the brigade is in this situation, that he's not been able to really defeat the column as he wanted to do, and, you know, noting the fact that the Muslims, you know, have done everything that they can to save members of the column to at least whatever degree they can. Now Pandurevic basically lays out his justification for why he has decided to open a corridor. And in this particular context, then -- now he's noting the col -- you know, the corridor is in his mind, I'm only letting the 500 civilians -- or 5.000 civilians out. So at this point in time he's now justifying his decisions related to why he let the column go. He notes at the back end of paragraph 3, which is page 2 of the English language translation, you know, the truce to allow the column to go out will succeed. He's still trying to push the issue of it's civilians, but he notes that a certain number of soldiers are likely getting out, but he's then claiming at the end, "Although those who passed, passed through unarmed." He notes that armed units have separated into smaller groups and are making their way separately. Paragraph 5, he's noted that despite everything that's happened, the overall front line from the Zvornik Brigade has not moved. They've not had to surrender territory, but you know, they've given up the line. And he notes that at some juncture he's going to seal off that area with new additional forces and again start sweeping the terrain, looking to engage whatever forces are not successfully let out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what about the last line?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again he's venting his frustration here. He understands that the rest of the Drina Corps is focused on Zepa and Stupcana 95. He's basically reminding the corps command, "I consider Krivaja 95 is not complete so long as there's a single enemy soldier or civilian behind the front line," you know, specific to him in -- in the Zvornik municipality. And at this point in time, even though he's let a large chunk of the column through, there are still hundreds, you know, maybe even over a thousand Bosnian Muslims from the column who were not able to make it out and who are going to be trapped behind the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could now have 65 ter 31137.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is an intercept from 21.16, the same day, 16 July, again related to the column being allowed through the corridor that Vinko Pandurevic opened. And if you could just take us through this, keeping in mind that we saw earlier the intercept from Drina Corps requesting that Popovic go check on Vinko and see what the situation is. This should be also in your tab 112.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have it. Here this conversation relates to the fact that initially Colonel Popovic tried to make contact directly with General Krstic and wasn't able to. So he is essentially briefing someone in the operations centre of the Drina Corps as to the situation. He notes that, "Do you know where I am," and they say, "Yes." "Did you get the interim report," and in this context they're referring to the interim report we've just discussed, the one for 16 July 1995. Popovic is basically acknowledging that, you know, the situation that he understand it is as Colonel Pandurevic wrote it. There's -- at the back end of it a phrase is part of the same conversation where all of a sudden Popovic says, "I finished the job," and the conversation is about "you finished everything." And it goes later that Popovic says, "I'll come up there tomorrow when I'm sure it's all been taken care of." You know, in this particular context you've got two issues being discussed. Most of the conversation has to do with the roles and actions of Pandurevic, but at the last part of the conversation it's my assessment that Popovic is letting the people of the Drina Corps to be passed to General Krstic, no, that the killing operation is concluded now as well, and in fact, this does correspond to the time of the last execution -- or mass executions in the Zvornik Brigade area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you which -- where were those on the 16th, the last ones that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the executions were completed at Branjevo, they still had, I think, the number is somewhere between 3- or 500 at the Pilica Dom of Culture, and so ultimately the last mass execution occurred in the village of Pilica where those Muslim prisoners being held at the Dom of Culture were actually executed at the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask kindly to have the rest of the Serbian version displayed, because I see that in English Popovic is saying that things were horrible, so I would like to see what it was that was horrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. If we could then show that to Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can read this part out here and ask you, Mr. Butler. Popovic says, "Well, in general there weren't any major problems, but up there, there were horrible problems up there. And that thing the commander sent it was just the right thing," so -- and then he says, "Just the thing. Horrible, it was horrible." So if you can, since Mr. Karadzic has raised it, what do you believe the horrible problems and horrible thing is being referred to, the executions or the conditions with the -- the situation with the column that Commander Pandurevic described in his interim combat report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context I believe that they are discussing the situation with the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And why is that? Why do you believe that that is the topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Previous page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this particular context, they are they talking about all through the day of the 16th of July, additional units are being brought into the Zvornik Brigade as reinforcements and it's talking about they're being sent up there. Well, in the context of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade as described to me by various officers of the Zvornik Brigade, up and down does not correspond to north and south. Up and down corresponds to -- the further west you go from the Drina River, you're going uphill. So when they talk about up there, what they are talking about in their vernacular is you're getting up there towards the front lines versus down there by the river. So military people generally, you know, they talk in the same vernacular. So I mean, the general appreciation is we're talking up there in the hills on the front line area when we're talking about, "They sent them all up there" and "the situation up there." It's not up there, geographically Pilica is north and Orahovac is south, something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? May I just suggest the following: Popovic says, "Horrible, it was horrible." "Horror" would be a better translation. Horror.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, the proper way to deal with it is to ask the CLSS to take a look into the matter by written filing. Mr. Robinson, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would agree, but I wonder if it's easier and maybe more accurate if the interpreters could just interpret what Dr. Karadzic read from the text and see if that concurs with -- maybe there will be no need for an official correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The only person at the moment that can read that part seems to be Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think, just in the savings of time, there is no reason not to do this and he can, of course, put whatever he likes in cross-examination on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, why don't we take this opportunity. Could you read that passage, Mr. Karadzic? Do you have that passage?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency. It's the first line -- or, rather, the second line in the Serbian version. "Horror. There was horror," or "it was horrible." I would like to ask the interpreters to do a verbatim translation of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Why don't you just read slowly so that the interpreters can interpret.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the interpreters may be able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They don't read for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So why don't you read from: "Well, in general, there weren't any major problems."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the previous page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Then why you don't read from: "Good," by Rasic. Do you have it, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I think so. Could I -- no, no. Here it is. Rasic says, "Good," or "all right," and then Popovic says something unclear, the first word. And then after the ... he says, "Horror ... there was horror."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or "it was horrible," interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Listen, Vujadin." Everybody can read this. Everyone can see that what this is is: "Horror."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We have noted that. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll check it, Your Honour, although the ... May I tender this, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4959, provisionally under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you could go to tab 19, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 1962, English page 3, Serbian page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is Commander Ljubisa Borovcanin's report from 10 to 20 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat the tab number, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, it should be one of two documents - probably the second document - in tab 119.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, 119. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, page 4 of the English. My mistake. Let me see which -- yes, page 4. Yeah, I'm looking for the entry of 16 July, which -- page 3 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, here the part I'm interested in is if you could tell us about the paragraph which begins, "At 1300 hours," where Mr. Borovcanin in his report writes Vinko Pandurevic and the commander of the Muslim side, Semso Muminovic, agreed to open a 1-kilometre-wide corridor in the areas of Parlog and Baljkovica to allow Muslim soldiers to get out, because that's different from the parts you highlighted in Vinko Pandurevic's report where he stresses civilians. If you could just give us your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, that is correct. Colonel -- this time it's still Mr. Borovcanin. Their forces were also engaged in military operations up at the Zvornik Brigade area and were part of this process and they were part of the forces that Vinko Pandurevic was using to fight the column. So as you can tell from -- if you look up one paragraph and look at the last line, at about 1500 hours, the bulk of the enemy column (his understanding about 2.500 soldiers) managed to break through to Nezuk. So Colonel Borovcanin has a different characterization of what the character of the column was or the composition of the column was than Colonel Pandurevic is reporting up his chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Might I tender that, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4960, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. That was the -- I'm now moving to the 17th of July, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 31265.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's your tab 115, Mr. Butler. Again I'll try to really quite quickly go through a series of documents again relating to Mr. -- command -- Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic's activities now on the 17th. So very quickly this first one. Can you tell us briefly what is going on here on the 17th of July at 12.42?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this juncture, somebody from the Zlatar command post either -- says "Zlatar 1," so it's either General Krstic personally or somebody saying Zlatar 1 wants to know where Popovic is. And Major Golic, who was at the Drina Corps headquarters, is reporting back that no, he's not returned back from Zvornik yet. He's still up there. And then the message is relayed. General Krstic ultimately gets on the line, as he's recognised by General Golic, says, "Listen, Golic, find Popovic, have him report to the IKM." At this particular juncture, the IKM that they're referring to is the Drina Corps IKM which is down by the Zepa area as part of Stupcana 95, and noting that, you know, "I want him here immediately."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I tender that, Your Honour, and then we'll go quickly to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4961, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have 31234. We have a conversation two minutes later, approximately, on the same day between X and Trbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is your tab 116, Mr. Butler. Could you quickly tell us who Trbic was in terms of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trbic, Milorad Trbic was a captain and he is the deputy security officer for the Zvornik Infantry Brigade at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, here they are still -- X is still looking for Pop, or Popovic. And Trbic says, "He went -- well, he went there toward that task north of you. Yes." And can you just tell us what this intercept is about, what is going on here that day?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an intercept between somebody relaying the message from the Drina Corps to the next lower level, which is the Zvornik Brigade, and they're asking where Popovic is. In this particular case, they specifically note the geographical reference "north of you." In this case, clearly Pilica, Branjevo, and the Dom of Culture are to the north of the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade. And they pass on the message, "Leave right away for here for Zlatar 1," he says. And the complaint that goes back later is, "I don't know how fast we can get to him because he's kind of isolated up where he is."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we'll get to that, but what is the situation north, Branjevo, Pilica, that area, on 17 July as it relates to Vujadin Popovic as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point on the 17th, they're essentially burying the bodies of the individuals who were killed on site at the Branjevo Farm, and they are also using military trucks to empty the bodies of those who were killed in the Pilica Dom and bringing those over to Branjevo so they can be killed [sic] as well. So there is a considerable clean-up operation going on in Pilica and at Branjevo for the killings that took place the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to tender this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. We'll admit it provisionally under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4962, provisionally under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I think before the break we can get through hopefully the next two related. If I could have 31191.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at your tab 117, Mr. Butler. Now five minutes later. X and Trbic again. X says, "It's changed again." "Yes," says Trbic. "If you get in touch with him, let him finish that work and then have him come here immediately. So let him finish that work he's doing and have him report immediately here at Golic's." What's happened here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For some reason that's not explained in the intercept, somebody made the decision that given what Popovic is engaged in, that someone in this context -- given that the order was given by General Krstic, I mean, he's not going to be countermanded by a lower authority, they've changed their mind and said, "No, I don't need to see him right now. Let's go ahead and let him finish what he was doing. When he's done, he needs to report here." The phrase "at Golac," I take to be Golic, Major Golic, who at that time is at the Drina Corps headquarters in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I tender that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4963, provisionally under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if you go to tab 118, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have 31223A, another intercept, 17 July, now at 16.22. Finally Popovic on the line. We can't hear the other person although Popovic refers to him as "boss." "Everything's okay. That job is done. Everything's okay." Skip a bit. "Basically that all gets an A, an A, the grade is an A. Everything's okay. That's it. Bye. Take care." So based on your understanding of what was happening at that time, being this time in the Zvornik Brigade area, what does this refer to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by this time the clean-up and the burial, I mean, it -- well, parts of it are still ongoing. Most of it's done. And this is Popovic reporting back -- in the context of this discussion, Popovic's boss is General Krstic, and reporting back on the situation. He's talking about, "I'm at the base." I believe in this context, I mean, the base that both Popovic and General Krstic would recognise as such would be the Drina Corps headquarters. So Popovic at this time is now back at the Drina Corps headquarters and he is telephonically reporting to General Krstic that they're completed with what they have to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I tender that, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we looking at the correct B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. I don't think that this is that version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, it's not. I don't -- the ERN should be 0080-1468 for the handwritten. So we must have a problem in e-court that we'll fix.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The wrong one --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. The wrong page has been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're doing that, it maybe would save time on cross-examination, I wonder if it would be possible if Mr. Butler could just indicate to us what he makes of the note: "French is heard in the background." That's something we may ask on cross but since it's here in front of us, it might be easier if he could ask that -- answer that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.text: Where where we, Mr. Nicholls?
