utterances.text: And French appears in this B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we upload the correct one now. Probably next page. Yes. Yes, next page. We can admit it publicly, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4964, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue, could the Chamber move into private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, before we continue, I just want to ask you about one answer you gave in the last session. This is at page 71, at line 17, and I just want to check if it's right. This had to do with Vujadin Popovic and the events at Branjevo on the 17th of July. What I asked you was: And we'll get to that, but is the situation north at Branjevo, Pilica, that area, on 17 July -- what is the situation, sorry, in that area on 17th July as it relates to Vujadin Popovic as well? And you answered: "At this point on the 17th, they're essentially burying the bodies of the individuals who were killed on site at the Branjevo Farm, and they are also using military trucks to empty the bodies of those who were killed in the Pilica Dom and bringing those over to Branjevo so they could be killed there." And -- I see you nod. Is it killed there or something else that would happen there to those bodies from Pilica Dom going to Branjevo on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should be buried there. All of the individuals that we're talking about were killed on the 16th, and they were subsequently buried on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 17th now still, could I have P02989.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at your tab 114, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is the republican communications centre log. And if I could have e-court page 16 in English, 7 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'm really going to try to move quickly this session, Mr. Butler. So while it's coming up, I'll tell you what my question's about. On the page that's coming up, we'll see that on the 16th of July, from the RS army Main Staff security organ there were reports sent to the Republika Srpska president, the Republika Srpska minister of the interior, State Security Service, sometimes attention Mr. Kijac, and Republika Srpska Ministry of Defence Pereula, which is probably Spiro Pereula. Now, I'm going to represent to you that for the 13th, 14th, 15th, 16th, 17th, every day, if we were to flip through this book we would see that this VRS security organ is sending reports to these same three principals. I want to ask you two questions about that. One, what can you tell us about that as an additional reporting chain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- can we see the B/C/S part?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. It should be page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One example would be the number 2351 in the left-hand column, for example. But my question, Mr. Butler, is: What can you -- what does that tell you about this additional reporting directly from the security of VRS Main Staff, in other words, Tolimir, Beara, Salapura, to the president of these other bodies? I'll just ask that first.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reflects that even though they were getting a comprehensive picture from the battle-field areas as a result of combat reporting from the various corps, the Main Staff intelligence and security department was also doing their own information and intelligence collection that was going up to the highest level of the government as well, the president of the Republika Srpska. So even within the army reporting chain, not only did he know about battle-field issues, but they were reporting to him on a regular basis, mostly it's once a day at least, intelligence information that the army intelligence and security people were able to derive themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My second question is: When you were working here and working on the Srebrenica case, were you ever able to find any of those security intel reports that went directly to the president?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, not with respect to any time during July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go now to 65 ter 02601.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is at your tab 120, Mr. Butler. This is from the 19th of July now. We're now moving on past the 17th. A MUP report from Dragomir Vasic. And I just want to ask you to comment on what this tells us about whether the forces of the MUP and VRS are continuing to take prisoners after the mass executions you've talked about.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Not only that, but as noted earlier, the column which was allowed to pass through once that 24-hour period was completed and the lines were --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask for -- for interpretation into Serbian. I can't hear it in my headset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right. Could you repeat your answer, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you hear in B/C/S, Mr. Karadzic, now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'll repeat. Even though the column was allowed to pass between the 16th and the 17th of July, once the lines were reclosed, it was recognised by the army and the police that there were hundreds, if not potentially more, individuals from the column who would be trapped behind the closed lines and that there would be requirement for various police and military forces to continue to sweep through the area in order to engage these individuals. This particular report on 19 July 1995 reflects that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And just before we move on, based on your work, what happened to Muslim men caught in these sweeps in the days just following the 17th of July, when the major executions you've described concluded?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time that the Zvornik Brigade begins to account for these prisoners officially is on, I believe, the 22nd of July, 1995. 22nd or 23rd, in one of those days' combat reports. There are reports of prisoners being taken on the 18th, 19th, 20th, 21st. None of those prisoners were ever accounted for. I believe that the answer on why they are not accounted for is that somewhere within close proximity of where those prisoners were captured, they were summarily executed by either the soldiers or the police who captured them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4965, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 13618, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is at your tab 126, Mr. Butler. And I'll just look at this quickly and then we'll look at another document. This is dated the 23rd of July. It's a MUP report from Dragomir Vasic -- excuse me, from Radenko Milicevic from the Srebrenica station, the new Srebrenica station, to the Zvornik CJB speaking about the 22nd of July. And it states -- it describes some problems with the army and states: "Deronjic has been informed of these problems. During the day he was in touch with President Karadzic about the problem with the VRS members." If we look at page 2 in the English. In the middle we see: "At last night 's meeting, Deronjic took it upon himself to obtain an order from the President of the country which will be sent to the local VRS command and will ban the theft of any property and putting of UNPROFOR bases under the control of our police forces." Now, before I ask you about that, could we look now at 13617. That's at your tab 125, Mr. Butler. An order from President Karadzic from 22nd July that appears to be about the same topics. And it's to the Main Staff, the MUP, and the War Presidency of Srebrenica, banning appropriation of property, et cetera. The question is: Looking at these two documents, putting them together, what does it tell you, one, about this other ability of President Karadzic to achieve information through a civilian channel, and, two, whether it shows that problems with the army can be resolved in this manner or as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, these two documents reflect exactly that proposition that local municipal authorities have an ability to reach directly up and contact the highest levels of the government, raise issues that are of significant importance, in this particular case the looting of the -- the abandoned UN supplies at Potocari, things of that nature, were deemed to be significant, and the president of the republic through his own orders process was able to issue relevant orders to all of the parties concerned, in this case the Main Staff, the police, and the municipality, regulating how that would occur and who would ultimately be in charge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I tender these two documents. Thank you. I tender these two documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. They will be all admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4966 and 4967 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Still now on communication in the later days. If I could have 65 ter 7586.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at your tab 127, Mr. Butler. That's an urgent notification on convoys from Drina Corps Commander Krstic referring to a call from President Karadzic, a personal call. Can you comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is similar to others that we've noted and intercepts that we've noted. When a particular issue arose that was of significant importance to the state, in this particular case dealing with convoy issues and the consequences of not allowing convoys to proceed unimpeded, President Karadzic, as the Supreme Commander of the armed forces, again would not hesitate to call directly down to the relevant army commanders in order to ensure that the proper instructions were given and that they were complied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Exhibit P4967 -- 68. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'll jump ahead a bit now. If I could have - excuse me - 65 ter 1908.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is at your tab 133, Mr. Butler. Another order from President Karadzic to the Main Staff. If I could have your comment on it and also perhaps quickly on what the military/political situation is around 26 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this particular time within Eastern Bosnia, we're looking at the end state of the Zepa enclave. Most of the military forces have been pushed back to the point where the enclave is no longer defendable. The negotiations have been underway for some period with respect to the ultimate disposition of the population. And in this context, President Karadzic is issuing an order to the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska directing, you know, which authority is going to be in charge of the evacuation of the civilian population and explaining why.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could tender that, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4969, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you go to tab 134, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I've got 65 ter 1935.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Two days later, 28th July, a document from Zvornik Chief Dragomir Vasic. And if you could just comment on this document, what it shows about the continuing tasks of the MUP units and PJP units regarding the -- the military situation. And also on the second page, when we get to it, subparagraph (a), if you could tell us what you -- what that means to you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. First part of the paragraph or first part of page 1, Dragan Vasic is recounting all of the tasks that his various MUP companies have been engaged in. Most of these run through the entire month of July 1995. And that they've been assigned all of these various combat tasks. And further noting that they're still having to deal with issues related to the Srebrenica problem where they're engaged in searching, laying down ambushes, and tracking Muslim groups that now at the 28th of July are still trying to make it across either the battle-field lines to make it to free territory or, as he notes, sometimes across the Drina River and to go to Mali Zvornik. And in this particular context, he is now complaining that he's just been told by the head of the police, Mr. Karisik, that he needs to deploy a company to another location for a seven-day period, and as part of that now he's recounting these are all the things our people have done and they're exhausted, and now I'm starting to have problems with, you know, issues related to desertion and things of that nature. The last part referenced in, I think, the last paragraph, subparagraph (a), he also uses this as an opportunity to note the particularly heavy toll that has been taken on the 1st PJP Company during the period, noting six men killed and 18 wounded, and also, you know, that they should be exempt from a number of tasks, and it also notes that because of its job at Konjevic Polje, this company needs a longer period of rest or it will fall apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I see that the job Mr. Vasic - and it's in the original - has put in quotation marks, what was the PJP doing in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that the 1st Company was in Konjevic Polje. The job in this particular context, I mean, there were one of two MUP units that were involved in the Kravica warehouse. One of them was the 2nd Sekovici Company and the second one was the 1st PJP Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4970, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now we're going to move into August, Mr. Butler, and discuss some issues which touch on prisoner exchange and topics like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So if I could have 31569, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at your tab 136. This is an intercept dated 1st August. I should have 31596B, actually. Intercept from 1st of August with one of the speakers being Beara from the Main Staff. And we saw in the Vasic report about some Muslims going across the Drina to Serbia. And we see here in the middle, "Listen, the men that you catch, hand them over alive to our men. We have nobody to exchange, fuck it. They've killed the Serbs and we are moving people out there and accommodating them across Serbia. That's what I've been doing so far, I handed over everyone I caught." And then the next speaker says, "And keep -- and do keep in touch. Beara is going to call you. Be connected all the time, and when you catch someone, they will immediately be taken over." And then later on, which is on the second page of the English, Beara comes on the line. Can you just tell us what the situation is now, this conversation about Beara and getting prisoners back?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this particular date and time, the Zepa enclave has fallen. The women and children who were in Zepa have been -- are being evacuated out, but the men, the military-aged men, for the most part are seeking to cross over the Drina River, the recognised international boundary, between Republika Srpska and Serbia proper. And what -- this particular conversation notes the fact is that the VRS is aware that several hundred so far have crossed the Drina River, more are following, and as they are being taken into custody on the other side of the Drina River, they're being handed over to the Serbian MUP, and the Serbian MUP is placing them under their control. So it's the VRS recognising that hundreds and later, you know, several thousand individuals from the former 28th Division who were at Zepa are crossing the Drina River and they're surrendering to the Serbian border forces or MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this intercept, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we previously indicated that we object to Zepa-related materials on the ground of relevance, so I think we'll object to this on that same basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I can respond to that. The relevance, I can make a proffer, is that at this time there's other evidence and documentation that the word of the mass murders in Srebrenica has started -- has been spread out. We saw that through all of Mr. Block's evidence. There are other documents I will get to and further documents, intercepts, in which it makes clear that Beara is seeking to get prisoners from Serbia, Muslim prisoners, to exchange. There were further documents where the VRS is complaining, "We have nobody to exchange." So the talk of the mass murders has gotten out to the international community. International organisations and the Red Cross are demanding access to prisoners and saying, "Thousands of Muslim men from Srebrenica are unaccounted for. You must have them prisoner. We want to visit them," and are being rebuffed. And at the same time, the VRS has nobody to exchange, where they should, if they hadn't killed them all, have thousands of people to exchange. So it is relevant to a -- one, to show what happened in Srebrenica, that all these people were killed; two, to show efforts to cover up the crime by desperately getting prisoners from other areas so that you at least have some prisoners you can point to to exchange; and three, it's the same actors, Beara, in charge of the murder operation, now seeking to find prisoners for the purposes I've just talked about. And we'll see in one of the intercepts, if I'm allowed to get it, Beara says, Look, why we can't we get these people - I'm paraphrasing - we weren't going to kill them, we're going to exchange them. So it is relevant. And the Zepa -- I don't have the cite with me but the Chamber has previously found that Zepa evidence is relevant to the pattern, plan. Zepa is part and parcel of Krivaja 95. It's part and parcel of directive 7, and so it's relevant evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And further, although they were talking about people from Zepa, the topic itself is not directly related to Zepa operation as such. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Mr. Nicholls' observation. We will admit this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4971, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have 31572A, another intercept from 1st of August, dated 22.45. Again, one of the speakers is chief of security, Colonel Beara. If we can quickly skip to the second page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is at your tab 136, Mr. Butler. I'm sorry. On the second page, S from the Main Staff after -- they're talking about how UNHCR are registering the Muslim prisoners in Serbia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think there is an English version for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's under 31572 without the A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: On the second page, and I'll ask you about the whole document, Mr. Butler, but S, Stevo from the Main Staff, says -- speaking about UNHCR registering the prisoners, says, "How can there be a decision when they're registering them? Beara --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Serbian page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It should be page 2 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Beara says: "They're taking their names, but that doesn't matter. We can, you know how, request that the ICRC escort them to us and they can be exchanged here as written in the contract. We had no plans to kill them, the motherfuckers, but to exchange them." And then it continues and there's a mention of Karadzic. So that's a part I would like to focus you on, but having read the document, can you give us your analysis of it, including the part I read?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Back on the first page of this document, this particular intercept, this is where they start having a numerical appreciation of the number of people that are ultimately making their way across the Drina River and talking about the fact that they're being filmed and that they are already under the observation of the ICRC, which leads you to the second page where they're talking about the issue of registration. In the vein of trying to camouflage where prisoners have come from and their origins for the numbers, they're already starting to worry about the fact that if prisoners are being registered in Serbia as coming from Zepa, you know, the role of being able to claim that these are Srebrenica prisoners is going to be more difficult for them. At this point Beara is not making it sound like it's going to be a problem because we're going to exchange them anyway, but it kind of makes it more difficult. What their hope was that without registering them in any way, the Serbian police and the Serbian border police would just essentially turn them back over to the custody of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just to be sure, how did you come to the conclusion that they tried to camouflage those prisoners coming from Srebrenica instead of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm ahead of myself a little bit, Your Honour, having read the whole body of documents. One of the things that will come out of that is that there will be continuing pressure down the line from various officials on visiting or where are the prisoners from Srebrenica, and there's a whole bunch of mechanics involved explaining -- or trying to explain to these people why they're not available at the moment or things of that nature. So I've had the -- to be able to look at these in the full context. I guess I'm a little bit ahead of myself on what that ultimately will mean, so I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And may I tender the document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4972, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, could I have 31577, please, an intercept from 2nd of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at your tab 138, Mr. Butler. And this one features General Krstic now the next day. Can you just give us your comment on this intercept.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular document -- and I don't know who Mandzuka is in context. I'm not sure whether I ever knew that or whether I knew it at one point and forgot, but certainly General Krstic is talking about the numbers of individuals. The context of the conversation discusses the fact that there's a concern about letting them cross over into Serbia, and that Beara himself at some juncture is going over to Serbia in an attempt to take care of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I admit that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could something be clarified? I think the witness said "individuals," not "kids." I heard the word "individuals," and according to the transcript, it seems to be kids that are in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't see it in the transcript, but I'm -- I don't think Mr. Butler was referring to children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, some part is missing from the transcript certainly. If you take a look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- line 1 on page 90, something is missing. But certainly Mr. Karadzic is talking about the number of -- yes, something is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll ask you to just repeat your answer. That might be the easiest, Mr. Butler. And you were just giving us your analysis of this intercept.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again to repeat, General Krstic is discussing with this individual Mandzuka. They're noticing in this one particular case there's over a thousand of them. The concern about getting -- letting them go to the other state. I think at one juncture Mandzuka notes that there are 2.000 altogether and it's noted that Beara was going to Serbia. So we're talking about the number of individuals who are crossing the Drina River from the former Zepa enclave and putting themselves in the custody of either the Serbian police or border police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I tender this, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4973, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now could I have 31579, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is at your tab 140, Mr. Butler, 2nd of August conversation between General Krstic and Colonel Popovic. And if you could just tell us, you've testified about this document before, what is going on here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean they're talking about essentially contact that in this case Colonel Popovic has had with Beara. Popovic notes that he's also reporting -- that he, Beara in this case, is reporting to Miletic, General Miletic from the Main Staff. They're talking about numbers of them, and one of the issues that is coming up is that the Serbian MUP is not allowing the VRS access to any of these prisoners that are now in their custody, and that is upsetting General Krstic, at least, who has expressed the desire that he as the Drina Corps commander wants those prisoners back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would turn -- tender that document, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This one has been marked for identification --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then shall we just leave it at that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Could I have 65 ter 23195, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at your tab 143, Mr. Butler. This is slightly out of topic, but going chronologically, 7th of August now. RS MUP to the deputy minister proposing that the following members of the RDB Bijeljina security department are rewarded money for their extraordinary contribution and engagement during the liberation of Srebrenica and Zepa. From Kijac, head of RDB. Can you just -- we've seen a lot of RDB documents, reporting documents, et cetera, and the information provided by the RDB. Can you just comment on what this document tells you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a recommendation from Mr. Kijac. It's his recognition that the services provided primarily in collecting intelligence information and reporting that up by the listed individuals, he considers that to be of extraordinary value during the Srebrenica operations and is looking to see about rewarding them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4974, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just intervene briefly. This was signed on behalf of Kijac. I think that we can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. It says "za."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it's written -- it's translated as well, "For."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 22827, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is at your tab 144, Mr. Butler. It's dated 12th August. RS government State Commission for Exchange of Prisoners of War. It's brought to the attention, we can see, to Radovan Karadzic, the president, and some other senior members of the government. And the subject is the concept for the solution of the issues with Serbs detain at the Muslim prisons. Because of time I won't go through this whole document, but could you tell us what it says to you in the context of the situation in early -- in mid-August nearly now.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe this document is dated 12 August of 1995. At this particular juncture, the Republika Srpska military and political leaders have come to the realisation that those Bosnian Muslims who managed to flee Zepa are not going to be turned back over to the custody of the Republika Srpska, especially those who had been registered by the ICRC or were being registered by the ICRC. There were cases where individual prisoners were captured, not registered and then turned back over, but this is a recounting from the State Commission exchanging for war crimes where they are talking about, one, their knowledge of how many Serbs are in various prisons in Tuzla and other locations in Bosnia and Herzegovina versus the number of prisoners that they have or recognise that they have in their custody and discussing modalities of exchange. And the striking thing about these particular numbers is the fact that they're talking in tens and twenties, or maybe a hundred, when in fact they know or at least significant portions of the army and the MUP were aware that prisoners being captured from the 12th of July, 1995, until the 22nd of July, 1995, are being categorised in their reporting in hundreds and in thousands. So what is striking about this particular document is when they're talking about prisoner exchange issues, is what they are not saying, essentially the elephant in the room is what about the 3- to 5- to 8.000 that we had in custody after the fall of Srebrenica, and where would they have fit into this process?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I tender this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4975, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'm close to concluding Mr. Butler. If you could go to the next tab. This is a simple question I've got, but I want to clear up this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 22828, please. That's a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's the death certificate of Gojko Simic, dated 18 August 1995. Now, can you just tell us, based on your work on this case and knowledge of the Srebrenica investigation, who Gojko Simic was, what battalion he was in, and what -- where he was and what he was doing on the 14th of July, 1995? I'm sorry, that's a big question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be the easiest way just to answer it in reverse. One the survivors in the Orahovac massacre in his statement to I think -- I'm not sure whether it was first the ICTY or whether it was the Bosnian MUP and later to the ICTY talked about the fact that he recognised the name of one of his execution -- not the name, but recognised the voice of one of his executioners at Orahovac and identified that individual as Gojko Simic. He provided background information which reflected the fact that he had worked with Gojko Simic in Belgrade years before the war. He knew the individual, and that is why he was able, even though he was blindfolded, to recognise the voice of that man. As part of the OTP search of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, a lot of the records that we were coming across dealing with 1995, one particular stack of records that we came across were certificates for individuals who had been killed in combat from the 4th Infantry Battalion in July of 1995. One of the names that we noted was Gojko Simic. So this particular document reflects the military particulars of Gojko Simic, where he was living in the Zvornik municipality, what military unit he was assigned to, and where and when he was killed. And there are supplemental information on page 2 and page 3 to include, you know, where he was employed in Belgrade. So this particular document, the significance of it is in effect it helps to corroborate the story of that particular survivor about the circumstances by which he would recognise Gojko Simic's voice and create his identity, and it further serves to put Gojko Simic in a military unit, specifically the Zvornik Infantry Brigade 4th Battalion, on the day of the massacre, which would be 14 July 1995, and then further serves to substantiate him being killed two days later in the battle at Baljkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4976, Your Honours -- 4975. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 76. Exhibit P4976.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 4976. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Last topic, Mr. Butler, jumping now to September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 1911. Which I -- sorry, I see is also P04592. It's been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is your tab 146, Mr. Butler. This is from the Main Staff, signed by General Mladic, to the Drina Corps logistics, approving five tonnes of D2 diesel fuel for carrying out "engineering works" in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps, and the fuel's going to Captain Trbic. It says Trpic. Sorry, I couldn't have said that. This is going to what it says is Captain Milorad Trpic. Can you tell us about this document, what's going on in September 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: First what's going on in September 1995 and in through October of 1995, is that the VRS after -- after the international community has publicly laid out the evidence that it has regarding the mass executions that occurred in the Zvornik Brigade area, the VRS -- and in the Bratunac Brigade area, too, the VRS undertakes a significant effort to go to those mass grave sites, to exhume them, to remove the bodies from those sites, and to bury them in remote locations in the Zvornik and Bratunac municipality in an effort to hide the evidence of those executions. Unlike the July 1995 executions and [indiscernible] of the logistics behind that where the troops were cataloguing fuel, vehicle miles, and those types of things in a normal manner, the reburial operation was done in a much more discreet manner. One part of that, obviously, would be to provide fuel to the various trucks and the various engineer equipment that would have to dig up those bodies which were dug up during evening hours. In this case, General Mladic is issuing an order to his logistics staff as well as the command of the Drina Corps, designating that five tonnes of diesel fuel be sent down to the Standard barracks in Zvornik and turned over to the custody of Captain Milorad Trpic. And that's the name that's used. In fact, the individual that it's going to is Captain Milorad Trbic, who is, as discussed earlier, the deputy security officer for the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. So right off the bat here, the fuel is -- it's not going to the chief of logistics of the Drina Corps. It's not going to the chief of logistics of the Zvornik Brigade. This fuel is already going to a security officer and it will be his job to make sure that the fuel is properly allotted for these jobs, and in this way, a lot of the evidence behind the reburial operation doesn't make it onto the normal books.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You stated that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Or -- it's admitted. Sorry. If I could have P04593.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at tab 147, Mr. Butler. Also 14 September 1992. Main Staff of the VRS logistics sector, 14 September, diesel D2, 5.000 litres. Could you explain this document for us. Same time period as the one we just looked at.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is related to the first document. It is the authorisation by the chief of the Main Staff logistics sector, saying that the fuel is made available for the engineering works and telling the Drina Corps and Zvornik Brigade that they need -- or in this case the Drina Corps representative needs to come up and collect the fuel and provide the transportation. Essentially letting them know that the fuel is now available. You know, bring a truck to bring it back with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I misspoke at line 12 of this page. It's September 1995, obviously. Mr. Butler, we obviously weren't able to go through everything that's contained in your military narrative report and your other reports that we were admitted -- that we've admitted in this case now, but we've gone through some vehicle logs, some intercepts, referred to fuel orders. The -- and you talked about the logistics required for -- that would be required for taking care of prisoners. When you look at the orders, the evidence in terms of fuel, requisition orders, vehicle logs that were in your report, military rosters and the intercepts and orders, how, if it does at all, does the murder operation, I'll call it, resemble a legal military operation in the way it was executed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that particular context, it doesn't differ at all. Soldiers, their officers, and the plans and procedures that the military, specifically the VRS, put in place, the military bureaucracy, if you will, that dealt with the legitimate aspects of the military attack with Krivaja 95 and Stupcana 95 were the exact same ones that were also used with respect to the executions. There are numerous cases where vehicle drivers, because they recognised that they had to fully account for the miles of their vehicles and what cargo was taken, are listing such notations as: Buses full of prisoners or a vehicle carrying prisoners on a certain day. Fuel being dispersed. Like I said, the scenario or the vignette that we talk about with respect to them needing an additional 500 litres of fuel in Pilica to complete the killing and burial operation up there on 16th and the 17th, even men as powerful in the security branch as Colonel Beara and Colonel Popovic had to go through proper channels in order to requisition fuel. There are notations in the log-book of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade where there are requests that is made for ammunition. This ammunition in some cases is used for these executions, because you have to have that done in a proper order. It has to be issued out from the armory, it has to be sent, it has to be accounted for. The fact that people who are driving the engineer vehicles that are involved in burying the bodies in Orahovac and Petkovci and Rocevic are accurately accounting for their time and the fuel that those vehicles are using, as well as the fact that the Engineer Company is accurately accounting for where those vehicles are used and where they are. So in that particular context, the same process and procedures that the Drina Corps, the Zvornik Brigade, and the Bratunac Brigade for the most part would use as part of their everyday military operations were also followed for their role in the conduct of the crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then do you mean to say that the killing order in the murder operation, so to speak, was conveyed or ordered through the chain of command in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would have had to have been. Certainly within the senior leadership of the VRS, which would be the Main Staff officers, the Drina Corps officers, their commanders, of course, and the key officers of the brigades, the Zvornik and the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So in this case, the killing order must have been conveyed from Mladic, General Krstic, and Colonel Pandurevic, or Major Obrenovic, and to the military police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, not in the sense that we can say that General Mladic personally called Krstic who then personally called Pandurevic, but through their staffs the relevant people were informed of what the orders were, what had to be accomplished, almost in a normal army commanding staff process. The people who were receiving those orders received what they believed were the relative assurances that the orders that they were given were the orders that needed to be carried out. Despite the fact that they were overtly illegal from a legal sense and while there were questions about carrying them out, the fact is that by and large people did not overly question the orders that they were given, whether they agreed with them or not, and in fact did so. So in that particular context, the military chain of command in that regard worked as it's supposed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. I don't have any more questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There were a couple of intercepts you would come back -- you will deal with it at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic, are you ready to start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Excellency, if you think that it is worthwhile these last 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karadzic. One further question for Mr. Nicholls. Were you minded to tender that sheet of paper referring to Mr. Butler's -- witness referred to in Mr. Butler's report, pseudonyms or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I didn't necessarily know whether we should formally tender it as an exhibit or just as an aide but I think it could be useful. Let me just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I think we need to admit, albeit under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we give the number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 4977, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, since we have very little time left, I would like to start from 1992 as well, just as the learned Mr. Nicholls did. Do you remember - I think you actually wrote about that - Podrinje, General Morillon? Do you remember that civilians were bringing pressure to bear in order to be allowed to leave, so there was even commotion on different UNHCR trucks so that they could leave Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it you're discussing the situation, roughly April of 1993, where various UN and other civilian agencies were seeking to evacuate the Bosnian population that had fallen in on Srebrenica. Yes, sir, in that particular sense there was a lot of confusion. I believe a lot of that is documented in the United Nations own report with respect to the events that led up to the creation of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of similar occurrences elsewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina, namely that as the enemy forces, if you will, were getting closer, the civilians were doing their best to try to go elsewhere? Also that there were even negotiations with the Muslim armed forces in order to have the Serbian side allow the civilians to get through.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can -- while not getting into specifics, generally speaking, there were a number of situations that I'm aware of where because of military combat operations, accommodations were made trying to get some parts of the civilian population out of an immediate combat zone and normally the United Nations played a key role in that, negotiating with various parts -- you know, the various warring factions. I don't know a lot of details about those types of things, but I am aware generally that the UN was -- was primarily involved in working with those warring factions to try and get civilians out of areas where they were perceived to be at risk from ongoing military operations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the witness now please be shown D1323 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, this was resolved two weeks before directive number 4, and it has to do with Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the penultimate page? I think that that would be the right order. So could we please have the penultimate page. The 23rd of October. The last two pages, please. Maybe the 25th. Well, yes. Could we have that in Serbian, please. Oh, yes, we do have it there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please focus on what the Presidency is doing, the War Presidency, or the municipality of Kotor Varos. They are in session every day, and every day they have minutes recorded. And item 2 says that Captain Slobodan Zupljanin pointed out that there had been no operations and that regular activities were ongoing. Contact had been established with Vecici, and a proposal was made to them to send a letter on behalf of the War Presidency offering the evacuation of their women and children to avoid their getting killed. In connection with this proposal, all the members of the War Presidency stated their individual opinions and the conclusion was adopted to issue a last call for the release of women and children and all our prisoners and then to deal with this military -- with this issue in a military manner. So, did you know that deep in our territory there were Muslim villages that had not surrendered weapons and that wanted to go on fighting and that Vecici was a village like that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that I was aware generally that there were at this point in time pockets like that as you've described, although I don't know this particular place or the circumstances behind it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page now. I mean, the session that was held on the 26th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The previous page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 11 in English in this document. Yes. We have the Serbian. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at item 3 now. Sub-item 3: "The final text of the call to the paramilitary formations of the village of Vecici for the evacuation of their women and children on the condition that the Serbian hostages be released."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the previous page now, the one before this one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 27th. Now look at item 2 -- paragraph 2. I see. "Lieutenant-Colonel Novakovic and Aleksandar Petrovic briefed the War Presidency on the situation in the field. "Zarko Mikic informed the War Presidency of the text of the call to the paramilitary formations of the village of Vecici and the same was accepted."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the previous one now of the 28th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Again item 2, there is a reference to the situation on the ground, and paragraph 2 says: "Zdravko Pejic informed the War Presidency about the results of the negotiations with the villagers of Vecici and proposed a solution. The proposed solution was adopted, i.e., to accept the evacuation of the civilian population on the condition that the hostages be released and then for the remaining part to be blocked by the army and destroyed. All the members of the War Presidency supported the proposed solution to the issue of the village of Vecici."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the previous one now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 29th, again item 2: "Zdravko Pejic informed the War Presidency that agreement had been reached with the villagers of Vecici to evacuate the women and children and Serbian hostages on Sunday."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the previous one now. The 30th of October. Again it is item 2: "Zdravko Pejic informed the War Presidency about the talks that had been held with the villagers of Vecici, as well as that two bodies had been pulled out." Can we have the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this too fast to you, Mr. Butler? No?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm following along fine, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see this now, the 1st of November. And it says Zdravko Pejic, it's underlined here: "Zdravko Pejic informed the War Presidency in detail about the course of events and the details of the negotiations with the villagers of Vecici. The inhabitants of Vecici. As well as the particulars of the agreement with Karadzic and General Talic." Then there is some discussion on this -- or, rather, some solution was adopted, but Major Trivic, please look further down, noted that things were clear and also that he was abreast of events that he had issued a written order and informed the corps commander accordingly. He believed that a mistake had been made somewhere along the way and that if President Karadzic has his own position as regards a solution to this problem, he should issue an order through Mladic and Talic which we would execute. He asked that nothing be done until he checked how things stood on the following day and informed the War Presidency accordingly and for the time being we were to prevent the armed forces from pulling out of Vecici until we received orders. Then it says further on -- I mean, there was this other discussion that ensued but that doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the previous one now. The 2nd of November. I don't think this is the previous one in English. Another page back in English. No, it was fine in Serbian. Page 3 in e-court in English. It's fine in Serbian now. I believe that this is good now. No, it's not. No, this is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. It says "Extraordinary session of the War Presidency continued." With "... Colonel Blagojevic informing all present that he had received explicit orders from General Mladic that no one was to be allowed to leave Vecici until the unconditional surrender of weapons was completed. "President Djekanovic concluded that there were differences between Karadzic's position and Mladic's order with respect to this problem. Major Trivic declared the position of the corps command that nobody was to be allowed to leave Vecici until the unconditional surrender of arms was completed and he proposed that this -- that they be told once again so that they might give thought to idea of unconditional surrender. He also remarked that President Djekanovic when talking to Karadzic should not tell him that his instructions were not being heeded but to try and convince him that the only right way to solve the issue of Vecici was unconditional surrender, and in that spirit he asked Djekanovic to help resolve this problem." And further on it says that they brought two Muslims from Vecici to negotiate and they sent them back to Vecici as well. And the first page is something we most probably don't need because there is no reference to this problem. So can you reconstruct this? Do you see that my position was to have them released, to have civilians released? Mladic's position was that they should not be released. Talic's position was also that they should not be released. And then in other documents we see that Mladic ultimately did agree to my proposal. Talic carried it out but stated his reservations that he disagreed, namely, and that this Muslim paramilitary armed group would remain behind.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it from the series of documents that, one, it seems that the War Presidency and the 1st Krajina Corps had a difference of opinion as to how the issue should be resolved. There was some confusion with respect to what the various negotiating positions were, but ultimately as described by this and in your own statement, once the issue of conflict between what General Mladic and General Talic wanted and the War Presidency brought their position to you, you ultimately made the decision, and as noted, even though General Talic did not want to carry it out, he did carry out the order. So in that particular context, even though it was November 1992, I take it that, you know, that is the way that this process was supposed to work, with ultimately the Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces, you, making the final call and the military personnel, whether they agreed with it or not, following your order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But the fact remains, and if necessary we're going to show a document tomorrow, the fact remains that the civilians did leave and that an armed force stayed behind, an armed force from this village. Can we see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't know whether that did or did not occur. I'm just not familiar with that particular area. If you say that that is the case, I -- I will believe you in the sense that the civilians were evacuated. That is something that obviously can be verified. So, again I don't know the details specifically, but it says what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tomorrow we're going to show another document as well, and then perhaps we can move on to directive 4, which has to do with these events. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it's time now, isn't it, Excellencies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, correct. We'll rise for today and resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
